Health and general fitness · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Garber 2011](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e318213fefb), [Bull 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955), [McDonald 2019n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/exercise-for-health-and-fitness)

### Occasional heavier sets and loaded standing lifts are worth including for bone

**Bone responds to heavy loading through the skeleton. A health-focused lifter gains from some sets of 5 or 6 without living there.**

In 101 postmenopausal women with low bone mass, eight months of supervised heavy lifting and impact work, built on five sets of five at over 85% of max, raised lumbar spine bone density by 2.9% while it fell 1.2% in a low-intensity home programme. McDonald advises people training for health to visit lower rep ranges from time to time for this reason, and to include lifts that load the spine and legs, such as squats or overhead presses. His caution is that constant heavy work wears on joints in older lifters, and that these lifts need competent teaching. Anyone with diagnosed low bone mass should be supervised.

- Include a few weeks of sets of 5 or 6 on a well-learned lift in each training block.
- With low bone density, start heavy loading only under professional supervision.

Health and general fitness · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Watson 2017](https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.3284), [McDonald 2019n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/exercise-for-health-and-fitness)

### After the first year, vary reps in simple ways

**Three easy options: step the reps down over weeks, progress inside one wide rep range, or use two rep ranges in the same week.**

McDonald suggests more structure only after 6 to 12 months of steady basic training. One option is to start at sets of 12 and move to 10, 8 and then 6 every two or three weeks, adding weight at each step, then take an easy week or two and begin again. A second is double progression in a range of 6 to 12. A third is one session in a higher range such as 10 to 12 and another in a lower one such as 6 to 8. He does not rank them: the best choice is the one a person will keep doing. A meta-analysis of 18 studies found periodised training produced larger one-rep-max gains than unvaried training.

- Pick one scheme and run it for several months.
- Take an easy week when a cycle of heavier weeks ends.

Health and general fitness · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2019n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/exercise-for-health-and-fitness), [Williams 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0734-y)

## Common mistakes

### Counting years in the gym as proof you are past the beginner stage

**Time served does not make a lifter intermediate. Stable technique, the ability to work hard and measurable gains do.**

McDonald's observation from two decades of coaching is that almost everyone rates themselves as more advanced than they are. A person can lift for two years, or twenty, and still have unstable technique, little capacity for hard effort, no added muscle and a disorganised routine. In his terms that person remains a beginner and progresses fastest on beginner training for a while. He adds that experienced lifters, like athletes in other sports, go back to basic work for short spells on purpose. A return to a simple plan is a normal part of training.

- Judge your level by technique and progress, then choose the routine that fits it.

Starting out · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015e](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training)

### Starting on a one-muscle-a-day bodybuilding split

**A split trains each exercise about once a week, which starves a beginner of practice and invites far more sets than needed.**

When weekly sets are matched, split and full-body routines produce similar strength and size in trials, so a split is not harmful in itself. McDonald's objection is specific to beginners. Each exercise comes round about once in seven days, so the movements are learned slowly. And because each session covers only one or two muscles, new lifters fill the time with exercises and sets they do not need. The only split he accepts for a beginner is upper body and lower body on separate days, used because it allows training two days in a row, and only with the sets for each muscle held down.

- Use full-body sessions for the first months.
- If your week forces a split, use upper and lower days and keep sets per muscle low.

Building a first programme · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Ramos-Campo 2024](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004774), [McDonald 2015g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/beginning-weight-training-3)

### Setting first weights from a body-weight formula

**Rules that tell a beginner to squat or press a fixed share of body weight fit some people and badly overload others.**

Some programmes give starting loads as a fraction of body weight. McDonald rejects the idea for beginners and for everyone else. Two people of the same weight can differ in age, sex, build, training history and how much of that weight is muscle, so one ratio cannot suit both. A heavy, untrained 55-year-old and a light 20-year-old athlete would each get the wrong answer, in opposite directions. Even where a ratio matches the average new lifter, an individual has no way of knowing whether they are that average. Trial from the light end takes a session or two longer and carries none of that risk.

- Ignore starting-weight ratios and work up from the lightest load.

Building a first programme · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training-5)

### Adding weight every session whether or not the last one was clean

**Plans that ask for more weight each time work when a coach makes the call. Alone, lifters keep adding after technique has begun to slip.**

Low-rep beginner plans usually ramp to one top set and ask for a small increase next time. McDonald accepts that beginners can ride this for a long while. His concern is the uncoached lifter, often a young man, who treats the increase as automatic. His own mentor's rule was stricter: add nothing until every set is completed under control, even if that means the same weights for the first month, and after that expect to add about once a week. McDonald sits between the two. He adds small amounts until the lifter can feel the lift, holds there until technique is stable, then progresses gradually.

- Add weight only when every set at the current load was done under control.
- Film a set or ask an experienced lifter to watch before raising the load.

Building a first programme · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training-6)

### Programming five heavy sets of five on every exercise

**Heavy low-rep sets need rests of several minutes, so more than one or two such lifts makes a session unworkably long.**

Five sets of five with a three-minute rest take at least 15 minutes for one exercise before warm-up sets are counted. Two or three lifts done that way fill 45 to 60 minutes. McDonald's rule for strength phases is to train one or two main lifts heavy in a session and everything after them with lighter loads and higher reps. He also keeps very low reps for multi-joint lifts, because singles to triples on a single-joint exercise load one joint heavily for little return. A review of rest intervals found that 3 to 5 minutes between sets allowed more reps across sets at loads of 50 to 90% of max.

- Pick one or two lifts to train heavy in a session.
- Do the rest of the session at 8 or more reps with shorter rests.

Strength and power training · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2014o](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-9), [de Salles 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/11315230-000000000-00000)

### Carrying on with jumps, throws or fast lifts after the snap has gone

**Power work only trains power while each rep is near your best. Slower reps add fatigue and nothing else.**

In growth and endurance training, fatigue is part of the stimulus. McDonald stresses that in power training it is not. Once bar speed, jump height or throw distance drops, the set has stopped doing its job, and when a new set opens with a flat rep the drill is over for the day. That keeps sets short and volume low, and it is why doing cleans or box jumps for high reps against the clock is conditioning, not power training. The 2026 ACSM stand found power was enhanced by low to moderate volumes with a fast lifting phase.

- End a power set at the first clearly slower rep.
- Keep jump, throw and fast-lift work early in the session, before fatiguing work.

Strength and power training · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Currier 2026](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000003897), [McDonald 2014g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-14)

### Holding off all jumping until you can squat twice your body weight

**The old rule was written for depth jumps, the hardest plyometric drill. Easy hops, jumps and throws need no strength threshold.**

McDonald traces the rule to a time when plyometrics meant depth jumps, in which the athlete drops from a box and rebounds. Applied to all jumping, it would keep many athletes from any explosive work for two or three years. His approach is to bring in low-level work early and in small amounts: ankle hops, standing jumps, medicine-ball throws and kettlebell swings, often as part of the warm-up before lifting. That teaches the movements and lets tissue adapt while strength is built. Intense drills come later. The cautions are to teach landing, watch for shin and ankle trouble, and do less when unsure.

- Add a few easy jumps or throws to your warm-up from early in training.
- Save depth jumps and loaded jumps until you are strong and well practised.

Strength and power training · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2014h](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-15)

### Switching to light weights and high reps to get lean

**High-rep circuits burn energy but hold muscle and strength poorly, and holding muscle is the main job of lifting during a diet.**

The habit of swapping heavy training for light, fast, high-rep work before a contest comes from bodybuilding. McDonald's argument is that it took hold in an era when anabolic steroids protected muscle whatever the training looked like, and that drug-free lifters who copy it give up the stimulus that tells the body to keep muscle. He grants that it uses more energy than heavy sets and empties muscle glycogen. His position is that it can be added in small amounts during a diet but must not replace heavier work, with complete beginners as the one exception. The diet area covers how heavy training protects lean mass.

- Keep your usual heavy sets when you diet, with fewer sets if recovery drops.
- Treat high-rep circuits as an optional extra, not the base of the plan.

Growth and endurance training · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2014b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training)

### Building high-rep circuits around technical barbell lifts

**Under heavy fatigue, squat technique changes within the session. Simple exercises are the safer choice for high-rep, short-rest work.**

Twenty-five people with at least six months of barbell experience did a highly fatiguing workout that included 55 squat repetitions. Knee and hip angles shifted, with less knee bend and more forward lean, and the authors concluded that such changes may raise injury risk. McDonald makes the same point from coaching: squats or deadlifts for sets of 15 to 20 on short rests invite a loss of form even when the load is light, and high-rep Olympic lifts are worse for anyone without years of practice. He builds these sessions from machines and other low-skill exercises.

- Use machines, simple dumbbell moves or easy bodyweight exercises for circuits.
- Keep squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts for sets where you are fresh.

Growth and endurance training · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Hooper 2014](https://doi.org/10.1097/jsc.0000000000000237), [McDonald 2014b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training)

### Doing three or four near-identical exercises for one muscle

**Barbell, dumbbell and machine versions of the same press train a muscle the same way. The extra exercises only add sets.**

McDonald traces the habit to high-volume bodybuilding of the steroid era, and thinks it leads drug-free lifters to do too many sets. His guideline is one or two exercises for a muscle in a session. The back is the exception at three or four, because it is several muscles with different jobs. Where a second exercise is used he wants it to differ in kind: a heavy compound lift, then one that loads the muscle at long length or one that is hardest in the shortened position. He keeps the same exercises through a block of six to eight weeks so progress can be tracked, and swaps them between blocks.

- Limit most muscles to one or two exercises in a session.
- Make a second exercise different in kind, not the same movement on other equipment.

Growth and endurance training · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2014l](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-6)

### Treating 8 to 12 reps as the only range that builds muscle

**Growth has been shown across a wide span of loads. The 8 to 12 range is a convenient middle, not a boundary.**

A network meta-analysis of 28 studies in 747 adults found muscle growth was independent of load when sets were taken to failure, while strength gains were larger with heavier loads. McDonald wrote years earlier that he could find no original research behind 8 to 12 as the growth range, and placed growth training anywhere from about 5 to 20 reps. He notes that Olympic weightlifters add size with sets of five. His practical limits are at the edges: very low reps need many sets and are hard on joints, and very high reps are painful and inefficient.

- Use any rep range from about 5 to 20 that lets you train the muscle hard.
- Choose the range by the exercise and by what your joints tolerate.

Growth and endurance training · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585), [McDonald 2014j](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-3)

### Taking warm-up sets close to failure

**High-rep sets on the way up tire you before the sets that count. Keep warm-up sets short and cut the reps as the weight rises.**

The old ascending pyramid starts with 12 to 15 hard reps and adds weight each set, so the lifter reaches the heaviest set already tired. McDonald prefers a ramp of short sets: roughly four steps from about half the working weight to just under it, with reps falling from five or more to singles, 30 to 60 seconds between steps and about two minutes before the first work set. Exact percentages do not matter; sensible plate jumps do. A squat trial fits this: adding heavier or faster warm-up sets did not increase the reps lifters could do afterwards compared with their usual warm-up.

- Do fewer reps on each warm-up set as the bar gets heavier.
- Finish every warm-up set well short of fatigue.

Warming up · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2009ai](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/warming-up-for-the-weight-room), [Souza 2024](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.17347)

### Applying the 20-rep grind to deadlifts or good mornings

**Technique in these lifts breaks down quickly as reps climb, and the part that fails is the back.**

Versions of the breathing-squat idea have been published for the deadlift and the good morning. McDonald advises against both. A squat that goes wrong late in a long set can usually be set down on the safety bars. A deadlift or good morning taken to that level of fatigue tends to finish with a rounded back under load, and he notes that one magazine author who recommended the 20-rep deadlift was injured for months by it. He tried it once and did not repeat it. Rest-pause methods on machines or upper-body lifts are a different matter, since a failed rep there carries little risk.

- Keep very long, all-out sets to exercises where a failed rep is safe.

Classic programmes and methods · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2016d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/all-about-the-20-rep-squat)

### Comparing your lifts with numbers that carry no conditions

**A lift only compares with a standard done the same way: same depth, no bounce or help, same body weight and sex, and no drugs or supportive suits.**

McDonald's test is to ask how many strict lifts at the 300, 400 and 500 lb (136, 181 and 227 kg) level you have seen from a lifter of about 90 kg (200 lb) in an ordinary gym. His guess is between none and two, because most big numbers quoted in gyms come from half squats, bounced or assisted bench presses, or much heavier people. Records mislead in the other direction: they describe the rare outlier, as the top tenth of drug-tested competitors shows with squats near 2.8 times body weight for men. A fair comparison needs the lift's conditions and the lifter's body weight attached.

- Record your own lifts to a fixed standard of depth and control.
- Compare yourself with lifters of your sex, size and training history.

Standards and time frames · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2011a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/300-bench-400-squat-500-deadlift), [van den Hoek 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.005)

### Judging every session by whether you set a personal best

**Records cannot come every time. Treating each ordinary session as a failure builds tension that makes the next one worse.**

McDonald's picture of the outcome-driven lifter is someone who must lift more than last time whenever they train, and who reads one flat day as proof of weakness. The usual response is to try harder, which tightens technique, spoils the following session and starts a run of bad days. He adds, as his own impression from coaching, that men fall into this more often than women and are less willing to take weight off the bar to fix a lift. His remedy is to change what counts as success: aim to do the movement right and let the load follow. After a poor session he often backs off a little or shifts the focus.

- Count a session as successful if the planned work was done with good form.
- Respond to a bad day by easing off, not by forcing a heavier one.

Goals and self-coaching · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2008o](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/goal-vs-process-oriented-training)

### Adding sets, sessions and exercises to your own plan as you go

**Self-coached lifters rarely fail through laziness. They do too much, too often, and explain to themselves why they are the exception.**

McDonald reports that experienced coaches say the same of themselves: they would never let an athlete do what they do in their own training, adding sets and exercises until the volume has doubled. His skating coach's blunt fix was to write the programme and then cut it in half. Outside accountability helps too: he had friends ask whether he was sticking to his plan. Supervision has a measurable effect. A meta-analysis of 12 studies found supervised training produced moderately larger strength gains than unsupervised training (standardised effect 0.40) and little difference in body composition.

- Write the plan before the session and do not add to it on the day.
- Ask someone to check now and then that you are following it.

Goals and self-coaching · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [McDonald 2019l](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/coaching-yourself), [Fisher 2022](https://doi.org/10.47206/ijsc.v2i1.101)

### Picking one habit of champions as the reason for their success

**The lifters who got nowhere usually had the same habit. What top performers share is a decade or more of consistent work, plus talent.**

McDonald's objection to the phrase about success leaving clues is that people choose the clue that suits what they are selling. Champion bodybuilders take supplements and train each muscle once a week; so do the far larger number who never succeed, and the champions mostly trained differently on the way up. A habit only counts as evidence if it separates those who succeeded from those who did not. His own list of what the best have in common is short: ten or more years of hard, sensible, consistent training toward one goal, and the talent that elite sport selects for. The rest he calls details.

- Ask whether unsuccessful lifters do the same thing before you copy it.
- Put consistency over years ahead of any single method.

Goals and self-coaching · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2011b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/success-leaves-clues), [Norton 2001](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200131110-00001)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6-12 months of proper training | Time before a beginner routine runs out: McDonald's estimate of when a beginner becomes an intermediate. The 2009 ACSM stand puts intermediates at about 6 months of consistent training. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2015e](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training), [ACSM 2009](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181915670) |
| 60 % of 1RM | Load that maximised strength gains in untrained people: Mean training load with the largest strength effect in untrained people across 140 studies. Trained people needed 80%. | Some support | [Rhea 2003](https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000053727.63505.d4) |
| about 80 % of the strength gain | Share of the three-day result from two sessions a week: McDonald's estimate for beginners training twice a week instead of three times. A coaching figure, not a pooled result. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2015g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/beginning-weight-training-3) |
| 2-10 % of the current load | Load increase once you beat the rep target: The 2009 ACSM stand's step size, applied when you can do one to two reps more than the target number. | Some support | [ACSM 2009](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181915670) |
| 10-20 % off the stalled load | Step back after a stall: The reset McDonald describes after two weeks without progress, followed by a rebuild over three to four weeks. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2015b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training-6) |
| 9-25 reps per exercise | Heavy reps per exercise in a strength session: From the old rule of 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps, which McDonald endorses for strength work. Stay low nearer 90% of max, higher nearer 85%. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2014o](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-9) |
| 6-8 seconds | Longest useful all-out power set: McDonald's limit for holding maximal power, after which output falls. He pairs sets this short with rests of 3 minutes or more. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2014g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-14) |
| 20-30 % off the working weight | Reduction from working weight for fast, explosive sets: McDonald's shortcut for lifters who train at about 80 to 85% of max. It gives roughly 50 to 65% of max, within the power range. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2014h](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-15) |
| 40-70 reps per muscle a session | McDonald's growth guideline for reps in a session: His working range at about 60 to 85% of max, citing a 2007 review he reads as favouring 30 to 60. Newer analyses count weekly sets. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2014a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-4), [Wernbom 2007](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200737030-00004) |
| 4-7 sets | Warm-up sets before heavy triples: McDonald's guide for work at about 85 to 90% of max. Sets of 12 at moderate loads need only one or two. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2009ai](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/warming-up-for-the-weight-room) |
| 75-80 % of 1RM | Load that allows five sets of five at one weight: McDonald's working range for 5x5 with the same weight. A single maximal set of five is about 85%. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2009b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/the-5x5-program) |
| 1.5 / 2 / 2.5 x body weight | The 300, 400, 500 rule as multiples of body weight: Bench press, squat and deadlift for a man of about 90 kg (200 lb), as McDonald works out McRobert's rule. A coaching target, not a norm. | Coaching practice | [McDonald 2011a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/300-bench-400-squat-500-deadlift) |

## Signs you have outgrown a beginner programme

Drawn from Lyle McDonald's criteria. Most of each group should be true before you change to an intermediate plan.

**Technique**

- Each main exercise looks the same from the first rep to the last
- You can feel the muscles an exercise is meant to train
- Weight has gone up for months without the movement changing

**Capacity**

- A full session of 60 to 90 minutes no longer leaves you drained
- Joints and tendons are free of lingering soreness at current loads
- You have trained two or three times a week for six months or more with few missed sessions

**Progress**

- You are visibly more muscular or measurably stronger than when you started
- Weights and reps have not moved for two full weeks
- A 10 to 20% step back and rebuild did not take you past your old best

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015e](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training), [McDonald 2015b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training-6)

## How a beginner plan shifts with the long-term goal

The base is shared. These are the adjustments Lyle McDonald describes for each aim, arranged here as a comparison.

| Long-term goal | Sessions a week | Exercise choice | Sets and reps |
|---|---|---|---|
| General health and fitness | 2, and it can stay at 2 | Machines or any simple mix that can be learned in a session or two | 1 set of 8 to 12 can be enough if it is worked hard |
| Support for another sport | 2 short sessions around sport practice | General whole-body lifts; bring in early any lift needed later | 1 to 3 sets of moderate reps |
| Physique | 3 | Free weights, machines and single-joint work; test which exercises suit your build | Build to 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 |
| Powerlifting or strongman | 3 | Squat, bench press and deadlift from the start, plus general work for the whole body | Sets of 5 on the main lifts for clean practice; 8 to 12 elsewhere |
| Olympic weightlifting | Set by a coach | Both competition lifts need a coach from the first session | Set by a coach |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/beginning-weight-training-3), [McDonald 2015h](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/beginning-weight-training-4)

## Free weights and machines: the practical differences

Results are similar, so the choice turns on practical points. These are the ones McDonald weighs for a new lifter.

| Point | Free weights | Machines |
|---|---|---|
| Time to learn | A barbell squat, bench press or deadlift can take weeks or months to learn well | Most can be learned in one or two sessions |
| Path of the movement | You set the path, so it can fit your build | Fixed by the machine; a poor fit can strain a joint |
| Balance and control | Trained by the lift; a barrier for people with balance problems | Largely removed, so effort goes to the target muscle |
| Tracking progress across gyms | A 20 kg (45 lb) plate weighs the same everywhere | Stacks and leverage differ by brand, so numbers do not transfer |
| Equipment needed | A bar, plates, bench and rack cover dozens of exercises | Usually one machine per movement; no problem in a commercial gym |
| Set-up time | Plates to load and more warm-up sets | Set the seat and move the pin |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2015g](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/beginning-weight-training-3)

## Dose that maximised strength gains, by training status

Mean values from two meta-analyses and the 2026 ACSM overview. The older analyses counted sets that were mostly taken near a repetition maximum.

| Who was studied | Mean load | Days a week | Sets | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Untrained adults | 60% of 1RM | 3 per muscle group | 4 per muscle group | Rhea 2003, 140 studies |
| Trained adults | 80% of 1RM | 2 per muscle group | 4 per muscle group | Rhea 2003, 140 studies |
| Competitive athletes | 85% of 1RM | 2 | 8 per muscle group | Peterson 2004, 37 studies |
| Healthy adults, all levels pooled | 80% of 1RM or more | 2 or more sessions | 2 to 3 | ACSM 2026, 137 systematic reviews |

Well supported · Sources: [Rhea 2003](https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000053727.63505.d4), [Peterson 2004](https://doi.org/10.1519/r-12842.1), [Currier 2026](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000003897)

## Kinds of training along the force-velocity curve

From heavy and slow to light and fast. Loads are from the cited reviews; the sorting of sports follows Lyle McDonald's discussion.

| Kind of work | Typical load | Example exercises | Sports that lean on it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maximal strength | 80% of 1RM or more | Heavy squats, presses and pulls | Powerlifting; linemen; a base for all power sports |
| High-load power (strength-speed) | Weightlifting exercises at 50 to 90% of 1RM | Power cleans, snatches, pulls | Shot put, rugby and football forwards, sprint starts |
| Power | 30 to 70% of 1RM, moved fast | Fast squats and presses, kettlebell swings | Most field and court sports |
| Low-load power (speed-strength) | Ballistic exercises at 0 to 50% of 1RM | Jump squats, medicine-ball throws, bounds | Javelin, baseball, jumping events |
| Speed | Body weight or a light implement | Sprints, unloaded jumps, light throws | Top-speed sprinting; racket and bat speed |

Some support · Sources: [Currier 2026](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000003897), [Cormie 2011](https://doi.org/10.2165/11538500-000000000-00000), [Soriano 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0341-8), [McDonald 2014d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-11)

## Load that gave the highest power output, by exercise

From two meta-analyses that sorted loads into three zones. The best load for power differs between exercises, so one percentage does not fit all.

| Exercise | Zone with the highest power | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Jump squat | 30% of 1RM or less | 27 studies, 468 participants |
| Squat | Between 30 and 70% of 1RM | 27 studies, 468 participants |
| Power clean and hang power clean | 70% of 1RM or more | 27 studies, 468 participants |
| Bench press throw | Under 30% of 1RM | 11 studies, 434 participants; results varied widely |
| Bench press | Between 30 and 70% of 1RM | 11 studies, 434 participants; results varied widely |

Well supported · Sources: [Soriano 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0341-8), [Soriano 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-016-0626-6)

## Three ways to count training volume

Each count answers a different question and each can mislead. The comparison follows Lyle McDonald's discussion of volume.

| Method | How it is counted | Useful for | Where it misleads |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hard sets | Sets taken close to failure, for each muscle each week | Planning growth training; the unit in recent dose-response analyses | Treats a set of 3 and a set of 12 as equal |
| Total reps | Reps for a muscle in a session, at about 60 to 85% of max | Comparing schemes that use different reps per set | Ignores how hard each set was |
| Volume load (tonnage) | Sets x reps x weight | Tracking workload on the same lift over time | Inflated by short-range heavy lifts and by large amounts of light work |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2014a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/categories-of-weight-training-4), [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w)

## Four kinds of weight training and the loading that defines each

Loads, reps and rests from the 2009 and 2026 ACSM position stands. The zones overlap, and most programmes use more than one.

| Kind | What it develops | Load | Reps and sets | Rest between sets |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maximal strength | The most weight you can lift once | 80% of 1RM or more (2026); 1 to 6RM emphasised for trained lifters (2009) | 2 to 3 sets enhanced strength (2026) | 3 to 5 minutes (2009) |
| Power | Force produced quickly | 30 to 70% of 1RM, lifted as fast as possible (2026) | Low to moderate volume (2026); 3 to 5 sets (2009) | 3 to 5 minutes (2009) |
| Hypertrophy | Muscle size | A wide range works; 6 to 12RM emphasised in 2009 | Higher volume: at least 10 weekly sets enhanced growth (2026) | 1 to 2 minutes (2009); the hypertrophy area has newer rest findings |
| Local muscular endurance | Repeating efforts for longer | 40 to 60% of 1RM (2009) | More than 15 reps (2009) | Under 90 seconds (2009) |

Well supported · Sources: [ACSM 2009](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181915670), [Currier 2026](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000003897)

## How many warm-up sets, by situation

Lyle McDonald's guidance gathered into one comparison. Heavier loads, more technical lifts and stronger lifters need more sets.

| Situation | Warm-up sets | How to do them |
|---|---|---|
| Beginner in the first weeks | None | The work sets are light enough to serve as the warm-up |
| Beginner once the weights feel heavy | 1 | About three quarters of the day's weight for 8 reps, then rest 30 to 60 seconds |
| Sets of about 12 at moderate loads | 1 to 2 | Light sets of a few reps |
| Heavy sets of 3 at 85 to 90% of max | 4 to 7 | Reps fall as the weight rises, ending in singles |
| Very strong lifter | Up to 8 or so | Bigger jumps early, smaller ones near the working weight |
| Second exercise for the same muscles | 1 to 2 | A short set of 3 to 5, then 1 to 2 reps, to find the groove |
| Sore or previously injured joint | Add 1 to 2 first | 10 to 15 easy reps with the empty bar or a very light load |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009ai](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/warming-up-for-the-weight-room), [McDonald 2015a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/beginning-weight-training-5)

90th-percentile lifts for competitors aged 18 to 35, from 809,986 competition entries, beside the McRobert target for an average man.

| Lift | Men, 90th percentile | Women, 90th percentile | McRobert target (men) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squat | 2.83 x body weight | 2.26 x body weight | About 2 x body weight |
| Bench press | 1.95 x body weight | 1.35 x body weight | About 1.5 x body weight |
| Deadlift | 3.25 x body weight | 2.66 x body weight | About 2.5 x body weight |

Some support · Sources: [van den Hoek 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.005), [McDonald 2011a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/300-bench-400-squat-500-deadlift)

## What a lifter can and cannot control

Lyle McDonald's rule: accept the fixed factors, use them only to shape your approach, and put the effort into the rest.

| Outside your control | What it limits | What you can do about it |
|---|---|---|
| Limb lengths and tendon attachments | Which lifts suit you and how much you lift | Adjust grip, stance and style; strengthen the weak part of the lift |
| Fibre type and how well you respond to training | Rate of gain and the eventual ceiling | Train consistently and judge progress against your own past |
| Natural hormone levels and age | Recovery and the speed of muscle gain | Sleep, eat enough, and match the workload to what you recover from |
| How appetite and metabolism react to dieting | How hard fat loss feels | Choose the diet structure you can keep to, and manage activity and sleep |
| Other people's results | Placings and comparisons | Set process goals and compete against your own numbers |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2011f](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/what-you-can-and-cannot-control)

## Weekly layouts for all-round fitness

Ways Lyle McDonald arranges lifting and cardio for general fitness, by the days available. All meet the guideline of lifting on two or three days.

| Days available | Layout | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Lifting and cardio in the same session | About 30 minutes of each; sessions run long but nothing is missed |
| 5 | Lift on 2 days, cardio on 3 | Lifting days spaced through the week |
| 6 | Lift on 3 alternate days, cardio on the 3 between | Equal emphasis on strength and aerobic fitness |
| Any, strength block | 3 to 4 lifting days plus 3 short cardio sessions | Run for 6 to 8 weeks, then switch emphasis |
| Any, cardio block | 3 to 4 cardio sessions plus 2 brief lifting days | The lifting is enough to maintain strength |

Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2019n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/exercise-for-health-and-fitness), [Garber 2011](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e318213fefb)

## Terms

- **20-rep squat (breathing squat)**: An old rest-pause method: one set of 20 squats with a weight you could normally lift about 10 times, made possible by standing with the bar and taking several deep breaths between reps.
- **Back-cycle (reset)**: A planned step back after a stall: cut the load by 10 to 20%, then build up again over three to four weeks and aim to pass the old best.
- **Beginner (novice)**: A lifter who still progresses on a simple, repeated routine. The 2009 ACSM position stand uses novice for people with no lifting experience, or none for several years.
- **Compound and isolation exercises**: A compound (multi-joint) exercise moves two or more joints and works several muscles, as in a squat or row. An isolation (single-joint) exercise moves one joint, as in a leg extension or curl. Both exist as free-weight and machine versions.
- **Double progression**: A way of progressing inside a rep range such as 6 to 12: add reps from session to session until you reach the top of the range, then add weight, which drops you back toward the bottom, and build up again.
- **Five sets of five (5x5)**: A strength routine of five sets of five reps on a few compound lifts, popularised by Bill Starr in a book for football players and revived by later barbell programmes. The label covers several quite different set plans.
- **Force-velocity curve**: The trade-off between the force a muscle can produce and its shortening speed: the faster the movement, the lower the force. Power, the product of the two, peaks in the middle of the curve.
- **General and specific warm-up**: A general warm-up is light whole-body activity that raises body temperature. A specific warm-up is progressively heavier sets of the exercise you are about to train, which also rehearse technique and ready the nervous system.
- **Hypertrophy and hyperplasia**: Hypertrophy is the enlargement of existing muscle fibres. Hyperplasia would be a rise in the number of fibres. Growth from training in humans is explained by hypertrophy; hyperplasia is unproven and, in McDonald's view, minor at most.
- **Load intensity and effort intensity**: Two different meanings of intensity. Intensity of load is the weight as a share of your one-rep max. Intensity of effort is how close the set comes to failure, often given as RPE or reps in reserve.
- **Maximal strength**: The greatest force you can produce in one effort with no time limit. In the gym it is measured as a one-rep max. Coaches outside the lifting sports often track a 3- or 5-rep max to avoid true maximum attempts.
- **Metabolic (depletion) training**: Weight training with light loads, sets of 15 to 20 or more and rests of a minute or less. It empties muscle glycogen and builds tolerance for fatigue more than it builds size or strength.
- **Myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic hypertrophy**: Myofibrillar growth adds contractile protein, the part of a fibre that produces force. Sarcoplasmic growth is a disproportionate expansion of the fluid and stored material around it.
- **Outcome, performance and process goals**: An outcome goal is a result against others, such as winning. A performance goal is a standard of your own, such as a 100 kg (220 lb) squat. A process goal is an action you carry out, such as hitting depth on every rep.
- **Post-activation potentiation and complex training**: A short rise in explosive performance after a few heavy efforts. Complex training alternates heavy sets with jumps to use it. A meta-analysis of 47 studies found small to moderate effects, larger in stronger, more experienced lifters.
- **Power (muscular power)**: Work divided by the time taken to do it, or force multiplied by speed. Lifting the same weight through the same distance in half the time doubles the power.
- **Prilepin's chart**: A table from Soviet weightlifting, attributed to A. S. Prilepin, that gives reps per set and total reps in a session for each band of intensity. It records what elite weightlifters did and was never tested in an experiment.
- **Ramped sets and sets across**: Ramped sets rise in weight from set to set, so only the last one or two are hard. Sets across use the same working weight for every set, after separate warm-up sets.
- **Rate of force development (RFD)**: How quickly force rises at the start of an effort. Sprint steps, jumps and throws allow only about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, so the force you can reach in that window matters more than your slow maximum.
- **Relative strength**: Strength divided by body weight. It matters most where you move your own body or compete in a weight class. Gaining weight faster than strength lowers it.
- **Repetition continuum**: The idea that low, moderate and high reps lean toward strength, size and endurance in turn. The zones overlap: the heavy end of size training is the light end of strength training.
- **Repetition maximum (RM) load**: The top weight a lifter can manage for a stated number of reps in good form. A 10RM is a load you can lift ten times and not eleven. A zone such as 8 to 12RM sets the load without a percentage.
- **Static, dynamic and ballistic stretching**: Static stretching holds a muscle at length without moving. Dynamic stretching moves a joint under control through a range that grows with each rep. Ballistic stretching flings the limb through the range and has fallen out of favour.
- **Technical failure**: The point in a set where good form can no longer be kept, even if a rougher rep is still possible. On skilled lifts it comes before momentary muscular failure and is the safer place to stop.
- **Training variables (loading parameters)**: The settings that define a programme: intensity (how heavy), volume (how many sets and reps), frequency (how often) and exercise choice. Rest between sets and speed of movement are often added.
- **Volume load (tonnage)**: Sets multiplied by reps multiplied by the weight lifted, added up over a session or a week. Three sets of 5 with 100 kg (220 lb) is 1,500 kg (3,300 lb).
- **Weider principles**: Names such as the superset, split routine and drop set principles, attached by the publisher Joe Weider to methods lifters already used. They are labels from his magazines, not discoveries; the hypertrophy area covers what the methods do.
- **Work capacity**: The amount of training you can do and recover from. Beginners build it slowly. Leaving every session exhausted means the workload is ahead of it.

---

# Technique: KiteSink fitness field guide

How to do the main lifts, and how to change a habit. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### For general training, bench with a part-tucked elbow and pinned shoulder blades

**A slight arch, shoulder blades held back and elbows midway between flared and tucked is a sound default for lifters who do not compete.**

This is a coaching convention, not a trial result. Lyle McDonald teaches most non-competing lifters a raw powerlifting-style press with less arch than a competitor uses. His reasons: it is kinder to the shoulders than pressing with the elbows level with them, it allows more load, and it trains chest, shoulders and triceps together. Feet stay flat, the chest stays lifted and the shoulder blades stay back for the whole set. Lifters with a history of back trouble can flatten the lower back and keep the same chest and shoulder position.

- Set the shoulder blades back before you unrack and hold them there until the bar is racked.
- Film a set from the side and from behind the head to check your elbow angle.

Bench press and shoulders · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2008b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/a-guide-to-bench-press-technique), [McDonald 2008c](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/bench-press-variations)

### Start and finish each bench rep with the bar stacked over the shoulders

**With the arms vertical the skeleton holds the bar. Lower it in a shallow arc to the lower chest and press back along the same arc.**

A coaching cue with no trial behind it. When the bar sits straight above the shoulder joint with the elbows locked, holding it takes little effort. Held over the face or over the belly, the shoulder muscles have to work just to keep it there. McDonald teaches a gentle curve: the bar travels down and a little toward the feet, touches around the lower chest, then goes up and back to where it started. He finds that pressing it all the way back over the face is usually too much.

- Check from the side that every rep ends with the bar above the shoulder joint.

Bench press and shoulders · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2008b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/a-guide-to-bench-press-technique)

### Pick a bench grip that puts the forearms vertical at the bottom

**Elbows stacked under the bar at the chest send force straight into it. Very wide grips add little load and may add shoulder risk.**

McDonald sets grip width from the bottom position: the forearms stand upright and the elbows sit under the bar, seen from the side and the foot end. Elbows behind the bar push it toward the feet, and elbows ahead of it let the bar fold back toward the face. A review reported that grips wider than 1.5 times biacromial width, the distance between the bony tips of the shoulders, may raise the risk of shoulder injury, and that narrowing to 1.5 or less changed the one-rep max by only about 5 percent. In 14 trained men, wide and medium grips gave similar shoulder and elbow moments at the slowest point of a max lift.

- Ask someone to look at your forearms from the foot end of the bench at the bottom of a rep.
- If your grip is wider than 1.5 times shoulder width, try moving each hand in a little.

Bench press and shoulders · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2008b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/a-guide-to-bench-press-technique), [Green 2007](https://doi.org/10.1519/00126548-200710000-00001), [Larsen 2021a](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2020.637066)

### To feel the chest in a press, think of bringing the upper arms together

**Focusing on the chest raised chest muscle activity in two lab studies at light and moderate loads, and less reliably at 80% of max.**

The chest muscle's main job is drawing the upper arm inward across the chest. McDonald's cue is to think about squeezing the upper arms toward each other while the elbows straighten, with the shoulder blades held back, and to learn it with a lighter bar. Lab work fits the idea. In 11 trained football players, an instruction to use the chest raised chest activity by 22 percent at 50 percent of max. In 18 trained men, focusing on a muscle raised its activity at 20 to 60 percent of max and not at 80 percent. Both studies measured muscle activity in one session, not growth over time.

- Before benching, press one empty hand forward with the other hand resting on that side of the chest.
- Take some weight off for a few sessions while the cue becomes automatic.

Bench press and shoulders · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2008d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/benching-with-the-pecs), [Snyder 2012](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e31823f8d11), [Calatayud 2016](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-015-3305-7)

### Stop upright rows when the elbows reach shoulder height

**Pulling no higher than shoulder level still works the side of the shoulder and avoids the arm position linked to impingement signs.**

McDonald's view is that the risk sits in the classic version, a narrow grip pulled to the chin with the elbows near the ears, and that stopping with the elbows level with the shoulders keeps most of the benefit. In 77 men, 46 of them lifters, clinical signs of shoulder impingement were associated with upright rows and lateral raises taken above 90 degrees. In 16 trained men, a wider grip raised deltoid and trapezius activity and lowered biceps activity. A shoulder with an old injury may still not tolerate the lift, and pain that persists should be assessed by a physiotherapist or doctor.

- End each rep with the hands around lower-chest height.
- Use a grip at least shoulder width, or switch to dumbbells or a rope.

Bench press and shoulders · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2012a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/are-upright-rows-unsafe), [Kolber 2014](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000000250), [McAllister 2013](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e31824f23ad)

### Finish every row with the shoulder blades together and the chest up

**The mid-back only does its share if the shoulder blades squeeze back as the pull finishes. A one to two second hold keeps that honest.**

Coaching practice. In McDonald's teaching, a seated row starts with a small forward lean and a straight back. It ends with the elbows just behind the body, the shoulders drawn back and down and the chest lifted, with the forearms in line with the cable. He likes a pause of one to two seconds in that squeezed position, which usually means taking weight off at first. The same finish applies to barbell, dumbbell, machine and inverted rows.

- Hold the handle against the body for a slow count of one or two on each rep.
- Reduce the load until the shoulder blades meet on every rep.

Rows and pulldowns · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009f](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/cable-row-technique)

### Inverted rows load the spine least; bent-over rows work the whole back hardest

**In a lab comparison of three rows, the inverted row gave the lowest spine load and the bent-over row the largest back muscle activity.**

Seven healthy men performed an inverted row, a standing bent-over row and a standing one-armed cable row while researchers recorded trunk and hip muscle activity and estimated spine load. The inverted row produced the lowest spine load, so the authors suggest it for people who want to spare the lower back. The bent-over row drew large, even activity from the upper to the lower back, with larger spine loads and the highest spine stiffness. The one-armed cable row challenged the trunk's resistance to twisting. This was a single session in seven people.

- Use inverted rows when you want back work with little lower-back load.
- Treat bent-over rows as lower-back work too when you plan a session.

Rows and pulldowns · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Fenwick 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181942019)

### In pulldowns and chin-ups, let the shoulders rise, then pull them down

**Letting the shoulders lift at the top and drawing them down during the pull turns an arm exercise into a lat exercise.**

McDonald's teaching points, which apply equally to chin-ups and pull-ups: let the shoulders rise at the top, pull them down as the bar comes down, think of driving the elbows toward the floor, and lift the chest to meet the bar at the upper chest. A slumped finish works the abdomen more than the back. Instruction can change which muscle works. Eight untrained women raised lat activity after technique coaching, at 30 percent of max, while biceps activity did not change. That was one session at a light load.

- Begin each rep by drawing the shoulders away from the ears.
- Stop the bar at the upper chest; do not push it down toward the lap.

Rows and pulldowns · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2009n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/lat-pulldown-technique), [Snyder 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181bb7213)

### Pulldown grip width matters less than gym lore suggests

**Lat activity was similar across narrow, medium and wide overhand grips, and the widest grip allowed the least load.**

Fifteen men lifted a six-rep max of about 80 kg (176 lb) with narrow and medium overhand grips and 77 kg (170 lb) with a wide one, and lat activity was similar across the three. In 12 men, an overhand grip produced more lat activity than an underhand grip, and width again made no difference. McDonald prefers a medium overhand grip or an underhand grip with the forearms square to the bar. He notes that the underhand grip lets the biceps help most and so allows the most weight. One-session muscle activity is a weak guide to growth, so comfort at the wrists and elbows is a fair tiebreaker.

- Use a grip between one and two times shoulder width.
- Pick the hand position your wrists and elbows tolerate best.

Rows and pulldowns · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Andersen 2014](https://doi.org/10.1097/jsc.0000000000000232), [Lusk 2010](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181ddb0ab), [McDonald 2009n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/lat-pulldown-technique)

### Behind-the-neck pulldowns add nothing for the lats

**Lat activity was the same in front, behind-the-neck and V-bar pulldowns, and the study's authors advised against the behind-the-neck version.**

Twenty-four trained men did front, behind-the-neck and V-bar pulldowns at 80 percent of max. Lat activity did not differ between the three. The authors judged the front version the best choice and the V-bar a fair alternative. McDonald's view is that the behind-the-neck pull mostly goes wrong when stiff shoulders push the head forward and drop the chest, and that few lifters have the shoulder mobility to do it well. Since it offers no extra lat work, most people lose nothing by pulling to the front.

- Pull to the upper chest with the chest lifted.

Rows and pulldowns · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Sperandei 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181b8d30a), [McDonald 2009n](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/lat-pulldown-technique)

### A deadlift bar loaded with small plates starts too low

**The usual start height comes from full-size plates, so lighter lifters need full-diameter light plates or blocks.**

Most lifts can be learned with an empty bar. The deadlift cannot, because the bar's height off the floor is set by the plate diameter. In many gyms the only full-size iron plates weigh 20 kg or 45 lb, which makes the lightest full-height bar about 60 kg (135 lb). McDonald points out that not every beginner can lift that in a good position. The fixes are light plates made to full diameter, such as bumper or technique plates, or resting the bar on blocks or rack pins at the same height and adding weight over time. This is practical coaching advice with no study behind it.

- Raise a lightly loaded bar on blocks or pins to normal plate height.
- Move to the floor once you can lift a bar with full-size plates in good position.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2008j](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/clean-style-deadlift-technique)

### With a mixed grip, keep the underhand elbow straight and swap hands between sets

**The mixed grip holds the most weight, and it exposes the biceps tendon of the palm-forward arm.**

Most heavy deadlifts are pulled with a mixed grip because it holds more than an overhand one. It has two costs. The pull is slightly uneven from side to side, and the underhand arm's biceps tendon is exposed. Surgeons reviewed 35 biceps tendon ruptures caught on video. Twenty-five happened in the deadlift, 24 of those with a mixed grip, and every one of the 24 was in the underhand arm. The authors suggest that gripping with both palms facing the body may lower the risk. McDonald's advice is to keep the arms straight and to alternate which hand goes under from set to set.

- Never bend the elbows to help a deadlift off the floor.
- Alternate the underhand side each set, or use a hook grip or straps.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Kapicioglu 2021](https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967121991811), [McDonald 2008j](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/clean-style-deadlift-technique)

### A trap bar deadlift shifts load from the lower back toward the knees

**Standing inside a hexagonal bar lowered peak moments at the spine and hip and raised them at the knee in trained lifters.**

Nineteen male powerlifters deadlifted with a straight bar and a hexagonal (trap) bar at loads from 10 to 80 percent of max. The hexagonal bar lowered the peak moments, or turning forces, at the lumbar spine, hip and ankle and raised the peak moment at the knee. Peak force, velocity and power were higher with it too. McDonald's view is that for most people who do not compete the trap bar is the better pull: the torso stays more upright, the thighs share more of the work and the bar does not have to pass round the knees. The study used submaximal loads moved as fast as possible.

- If your gym has a trap bar and you do not compete, consider it as your main deadlift.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [Swinton 2011](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e3181e73f87), [McDonald 2020j](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/you-must-squat-dsfps-2)

### A Romanian deadlift ends where the hips stop moving

**Any depth gained after the hips stop comes from rounding the lower back, which takes the load off the hamstrings.**

Coaching practice. In a Romanian deadlift the knees stay slightly bent, about 10 to 20 degrees, the hips push back and the bar slides down the thighs with the back flat. McDonald's rule is to lower only as far as the hips can hinge. For most people that puts the bar a little below the kneecap; long arms or loose hamstrings allow more. Signs of going past it: the pull leaves the hamstrings and moves into the lower back, the knees bend further, or you can no longer see yourself in a mirror because the head has dropped. Stiff lifters can stop higher and let the range grow over the weeks.

- Keep the lats tight and the bar touching the legs all the way.
- End the rep when the hips stop travelling back.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009ab](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/romanian-deadlift-vs-sldl)

### Use Romanian deadlifts for moderate reps and build up slowly

**Sets of five to eight after the main lift suit most people. Do not test a one-rep max, and expect sore hamstrings at first.**

McDonald's programming advice, from coaching and not from trials. Use the Romanian deadlift as a second lower-body exercise after squats or deadlifts, mostly for five to eight reps or more. He sees no reason to go under three reps and would not test a max, because position is hard to hold with near-maximal loads. The lower back works hard to stay still, so after heavy deadlifts or low-bar squats it may give out first. In that case go lighter or move the lift to another day. The loaded stretch makes the hamstrings very sore in new or returning lifters.

- Begin with a load you could lift for several more reps and add weight over two to three weeks.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009ab](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/romanian-deadlift-vs-sldl)

### A back that rounds mid-lift is a fault; a set, held upper-back curve is a style

**Arguments over round-back deadlifts mix up losing a flat back under load with choosing a fixed upper-back curve before the pull.**

McDonald separates two things. In one, a lifter means to stay flat and the whole spine, lower back included, bends once the bar moves. He treats that as a loss of position that shifts load from muscle to ligaments and discs. In the other, a skilled powerlifter sets a rounded upper back before pulling, keeps the lower back flat and holds that shape to lockout. He treats that as a trained style for advanced lifters. X-ray video of four national-class powerlifters lifting 184 to 211 kg (405 to 465 lb) found that, in all but one trial, the lumbar spine stayed 1.5 to 13 degrees short of full flexion.

- If your back changes shape during a rep, lower the load and rebuild the position.
- Learn the flat-backed pull before experimenting with anything else.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2015r](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/another-look-round-backed-deadlifts), [Cholewicki 1992](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9290(92)90242-s)

### Evidence on lifting with a rounded lower back is mixed and mostly indirect

**Tissue studies link repeated loaded bending to disc injury, while a review of people lifting found no clear link between lumbar flexion and back pain.**

McDonald advises against heavy stiff-legged deadlifts with a rounded back, citing spine research. The lab basis exists: pig spine segments put through highly repetitive bending and straightening under modest compression developed disc herniations, more often and more severely as compression rose. Near a full bend the back muscles also go quiet and passive tissues take more load. Human data are less clear. A 2020 review of 11 studies found low-quality evidence that greater lumbar flexion during lifting was not a risk factor for low back pain. His articles predate that review.

- Treat a flat lower back as the default for heavy hinging.
- See a physiotherapist or doctor about back pain that persists.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [Callaghan 2001](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0268-0033(00)00063-2), [Saraceni 2020](https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2020.9218), [Colloca 2005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmpt.2005.08.005), [McDonald 2009ab](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/romanian-deadlift-vs-sldl)

### Pad height decides whether a back extension trains the hips or the spinal muscles

**With the pad below the hip crease the hips do the moving. With the pelvis pinned on the pad, the spinal muscles must.**

On a back extension bench, where the pad meets the pelvis sets what can move. If the pad is low enough for the pelvis to tip over its edge, the glutes and hamstrings extend the hips; keep the back flat and the spinal muscles only hold, like a machine Romanian deadlift. If the pelvis rests on the pad, the hips are blocked and the only way to move is to curl and uncurl the spine, which takes the spinal muscles through a range. McDonald uses the second set-up when the hamstrings have already been trained. A review of lumbar extensor exercise agrees that restraining the pelvis matters for targeting those muscles.

- Decide which you want to train before you set the pad.
- Pin the pelvis on the pad when you want the lower back muscles to do the moving.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2009d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/back-extension-technique), [Steele 2013](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2013-092197)

### Start back extensions with one easy set and progress in small steps

**McDonald starts beginners on a single set of five to eight reps and keeps direct lower-back work well short of failure.**

Coaching practice with no trial behind it. The lower back is often weak in new lifters, so McDonald begins with one set of five to eight reps even if more feels possible, checks for back soreness the next day and adds a couple of reps per session. At twelve easy reps he makes the lift harder or adds a second set. Hand position sets the difficulty without any weight: arms by the sides is easiest, then crossed on the chest, then by the head, then reaching overhead. After that, hold a dumbbell at the chest. He places the exercise late in a session and leaves several reps in reserve.

- First session: one set of five to eight reps with the hands by your sides or on the chest.
- Add load only once twelve reps feel easy.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/back-extension-technique)

### Back muscle endurance was linked to fewer first-time back problems in men

**In a Danish population study, men with good isometric back endurance were less likely to report low-back trouble for the first time.**

A health survey examined 449 men and 479 women aged 30, 40, 50 or 60 and followed them for a year. Good isometric endurance of the back muscles appeared to protect men against a first episode of low-back trouble, and men with very mobile backs were more likely to have one. Among people with earlier back trouble, the main predictor of more was how recent the last episode had been. McDonald draws on this line of research when he programs higher-rep back extensions with a hold of two to six seconds at the top. The study was observational, so it cannot show that building endurance prevents back pain.

- Include some higher-rep sets with a short hold at the top.
- Keep those sets several reps short of failure.

Deadlifts and back extensions · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Biering-Sørensen 1984](https://doi.org/10.1097/00007632-198403000-00002), [McDonald 2009d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/back-extension-technique)

### Choose a squat style from your goal and your build

**A higher bar and upright trunk bias the thighs. A lower bar with more sit-back spreads the work to hips and back and allows more load.**

McDonald's answer to which squat is best is that it depends on the lifter. For a general trainee he leans toward a moderate low-bar squat, taken just below parallel with a stance around shoulder width, because it balances the muscle trained against the load lifted. A high-bar squat with a narrower stance, an upright trunk and full depth suits weightlifters and people chasing thigh size, and works best in heeled shoes. A biomechanics review supports the basic contrast between the two bar positions. Competition detail sits in the powerlifting section.

- Try each bar position for a few weeks and keep the one you can load steadily and feel in the target muscles.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2011d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/the-best-way-to-squat), [Glassbrook 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000002007)

### A raised heel lets the knees travel forward and the trunk stay more upright

**In two lab studies, weightlifting shoes reduced forward lean or increased knee bend compared with ordinary trainers.**

Twenty-five people squatting 60 percent of max leaned forward less in weightlifting shoes than in running shoes, though the thighs did not get closer to horizontal. In 32 people, weightlifting shoes reduced the ankle bend needed and increased knee bend, with a more upright trunk in the unloaded squat, and experienced squatters gained more from them than novices. McDonald suggests a heeled shoe for high-bar squats and for long-thighed lifters who fold forward, even in a low-bar squat. Both studies measured positions in one session, not strength or injury.

- If you tip forward in flat shoes, test a heeled lifting shoe before changing anything else.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Sato 2012](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e318218dd64), [Legg 2017](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2016.1175652), [McDonald 2011d](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/the-best-way-to-squat)

### Some lifters squat upright and some fold forward

**Lifters who lean far forward tend to tire in the lower back before the thighs. Ankle mobility is one measured cause; proportions are a likely one.**

McDonald's observation is that lifters with short thighs and a long torso stay upright and get strong thigh work from squats, while long-thighed lifters tip forward until the squat resembles a good morning and the lower back gives out first. The geometry is sound, but direct evidence is thin. In 11 men squatting to parallel at about 75 percent of max, greater ankle mobility went with a more upright trunk, while the ratios between trunk, thigh and shin lengths showed no significant link with trunk angle. Eleven people is a small sample for a question about body proportions.

- Film a squat from the side and note what fails first: thighs or lower back.
- Try a raised heel and a slightly wider stance before deciding the squat does not suit you.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2009ad](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/squat-or-leg-press-for-big-legs), [Fuglsang 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001872)

### Full squats grew glutes and inner thighs more than half squats; quadriceps grew the same

**Over 10 weeks, deeper squats gave two to three times the glute and adductor growth, with no extra growth at the front of the thigh.**

Seventeen men trained full squats or half squats twice a week for 10 weeks, with muscle volume measured by MRI. The knee extensors, the quadriceps group, grew 4.9 percent with full squats and 4.6 percent with half squats. Glute volume rose 6.7 percent against 2.2 percent and adductor volume 6.2 against 2.7 percent, both significantly more with full squats. The rectus femoris, the one quadriceps muscle that also crosses the hip, and the hamstrings did not grow in either group. On this evidence a squat trains the thighs, glutes and inner thighs, and the hamstrings need another lift.

- Squat as deep as you can hold position if glute size is a goal.
- Add a leg curl or a hip hinge for the hamstrings.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Kubo 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y)

### Squats carried over to jumping better than leg presses

**Eight weeks of squats raised jump height about 12 percent, against 0.5 to 3.5 percent for the leg press. For thigh size the leg press is a fair substitute.**

Seventy-eight students were split between training and control groups. Those who trained the parallel squat for eight weeks improved squat-jump height by 12.4 percent and countermovement-jump height by 12.0 percent. Those on a leg press improved by 3.5 and 0.5 percent, changes that were not significant. In 10 experienced lifters, the squat produced more quadriceps and hamstring activity and higher knee forces than the leg press. McDonald's case for the leg press concerns muscle size: it removes the lower back as the weak link, so the thighs can be taken close to failure. Neither study compared thigh growth.

- Squat if jumping or squat strength is the goal.
- Use the leg press as the main thigh lift if your back fails first in squats, or straight after squats.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Wirth 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001228), [Escamilla 2001](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-200109000-00020), [McDonald 2009ad](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/squat-or-leg-press-for-big-legs)

### On the leg press, go deep but stop before the pelvis rolls off the pad

**Bend the knees to a right angle or more, and treat the point where the lower back starts to round as the bottom.**

McDonald's coaching points. Loading every plate and moving the sled a short distance puts little tension on the thighs. He wants the knees bent to a right angle or more, which for many people means taking off about half the weight, and a short stop at the bottom to remove the bounce. The leg press does not protect the back by default. If the sled comes deeper than your hips allow, the pelvis tucks under and the lower back rounds against a heavy load. He dislikes vertical leg presses for this reason and notes that single-leg pressing, the free foot resting on the floor, makes rounding hard to do.

- Set the safety stops just above the depth where your hips begin to tuck.
- Try single-leg presses if your lower back rounds when you use both legs.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2009ad](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/squat-or-leg-press-for-big-legs)

### Set a split squat long enough and wide enough

**Both knees should be near a right angle in the low position, with the feet about hip width apart and not on one line.**

Coaching practice, and it applies to lunges too. Take a stride long enough that both knees bend to roughly a right angle at the bottom, with the back knee just short of the floor. A back foot placed too close folds that knee sharply. Seen from behind, keep the feet about hip width apart. Feet on one line, as if on a tightrope, make balance hard, and a back leg angled out to the side strains its knee. Keep the chest up. McDonald finds very low reps work poorly in this lift and uses sets of five or more.

- Mark your foot positions on the floor once you find a stride that works.
- Lower until the back knee almost touches, then stand.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2010q](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/split-squat-technique)

### Front shin angle steers a split squat toward the thighs or the glutes

**Letting the front knee travel forward biases the thigh. A vertical shin with the weight on the heel biases the glutes.**

McDonald describes three versions set by the front foot. Knee well forward with pressure on the ball of the foot is thigh-dominant. Shin upright with the hips sitting back and pressure on the heel is glute-dominant. Pressure at mid-foot sits between the two. A motion-capture study of 11 people carrying 25 percent of body weight found that changing the front shin angle and the step length altered the range of motion and the moments at both knees and hips, while the share of load between the legs shifted by less than 25 percent. Holding the bar on the front of the shoulders adds thigh work.

- Pick the version that matches the muscle you want and keep the foot pressure the same on every rep.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2010q](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/split-squat-technique), [Schütz 2014](https://doi.org/10.1123/jab.2013-0175)

### Rear-foot-elevated split squats matched back squats over five weeks in young rugby players

**Strength, 40 m sprint and agility improved equally whether the players trained only split squats or only back squats.**

Eighteen academy rugby players were randomly assigned to train either the rear-foot-elevated split squat or the back squat for five weeks. Both groups improved back squat max, split squat max, 40 m sprint time and a change-of-direction test, with no significant difference between them; 10 m sprint time did not change. McDonald uses split squats when the lower back limits the squat, after deadlifts, when only light weights are to hand, or to even out a weaker leg. He warns that the lift is not always light: the range is shorter than a deep squat, and some lifters handle loads close to their back squat.

- Use split squats as a main leg lift when your lower back needs a rest from heavy squats.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Speirs 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001096), [McDonald 2010q](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/split-squat-technique)

### In single-leg work, start with the weaker side and rest before switching

**Let the weaker leg set the reps for both, and take about a minute between legs so the second one is not short-changed.**

Coaching practice. Switching legs without a break leaves the second leg working while you are still out of breath, so McDonald rests about a minute after each leg and alternates until every set is done. Where one side is weaker, he starts with it and stops the stronger side at the same number of reps, even if more are possible. Another option is one or two extra sets for the weak side only. The price of single-leg training is time, since the same number of sets takes about twice as long.

- Count the reps your weaker leg manages and match them on the other side.

Squats, leg press and split squats · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2010q](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/split-squat-technique)

### Pause at the bottom of calf raises so the muscle does the lifting

**The Achilles tendon hands back stored energy when a rep is bounced. A two-second pause in the stretch removes most of that help.**

Tendons behave like springs: stretched quickly, they give energy back. In 10 men hopping on one leg, recoil of the Achilles tendon returned an average of 38 joules, 16 percent of the mechanical work of each hop. McDonald's explanation for thin calves that move huge loads is that fast, bouncing reps let the tendon do part of the work. His fix is a pause of about two seconds at the bottom, a short squeeze at the top and a controlled lowering. He warns against forcing the heel as low as it will go, and advises starting well below your usual load because paused calf work causes marked soreness.

- Count two seconds in the stretched position on every rep.
- Start with much less than your usual load the first time you try paused reps.

Calves and leg extensions · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [McDonald 2009ah](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/training-the-calves), [Lichtwark 2005](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.01950)

### Standing calf raises grew the calf far more than seated ones

**With the knee straight both calf muscles grew. With the knee bent only the soleus did, and no more than it did standing.**

The gastrocnemius crosses the knee, so bending the knee slackens it and leaves most of the work to the deeper soleus. That anatomy is why McDonald's 2009 calf routine pairs heavy, paused straight-knee raises with higher-rep bent-knee raises, twice a week. A later trial tested it. Fourteen untrained adults trained one leg standing and the other seated for 12 weeks. Standing raises grew the lateral gastrocnemius 12.4 percent against 1.7 percent seated, and the medial 9.2 against 0.6 percent. The soleus grew about the same either way, 2.1 and 2.9 percent. On this evidence the standing raise covers both muscles.

- Make a straight-knee calf raise your main calf exercise.
- Treat seated raises as optional extra work for the soleus.

Calves and leg extensions · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [Kinoshita 2023](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106), [McDonald 2009ah](https://bodyrecomposition.com/muscle-gain/training-the-calves)

### Why high-rep leg extensions burn so much is not established

**McDonald's guess is that the seated, hip-bent position limits blood flow through the thigh for the whole set. Nobody has tested it.**
