# Powerlifting: KiteSink fitness field guide

A bigger squat, bench press and deadlift. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### Heavy loads build strength better than light loads

**For strength, heavy and moderate loads beat light loads, so most working sets should sit in the heavy to moderate range.**

A network meta-analysis of 28 studies in 747 healthy adults, all taken to failure, found muscle growth was similar across loads. Strength gains were larger with high loads (8 repetitions or fewer to failure) and moderate loads (9 to 15) than with low loads (over 15). High versus moderate was not clearly different. Light work still has a place for skill and recovery.

- Keep most working sets on the competition lifts in the 1-8 repetition range.
- Use light sets for warm-ups, skill work and easy days.

Percentages and zones · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Lopez 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0000000000002585)

### Practise the lifts in competition style and hold four principles

**Strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift is partly skill, so the lifts themselves, done to competition standard, make up most of the training.**

This is coaching convention, not a trial result. Train squat depth, the bench pause and the deadlift lockout the way they are judged. Four principles carry across the lifts: a stable base, full-body tightness before the bar moves, a planned bar path, and the same set-up every rep. In the squat and deadlift that path stays close to a straight line over mid-foot. The bench differs: McDonald teaches a shallow arc, with the bar touching low on the chest and finishing above the shoulders. Assistance exercises support the lifts and do not replace them.

- Film your heaviest set of each lift every week, from the side.
- Use the same set-up routine on warm-ups and on heavy sets.

Technique and leverages · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [McDonald 2008b](https://bodyrecomposition.com/training/a-guide-to-bench-press-technique)

### RPE with reps in reserve lets you pick the load by feel

**A set rated RPE 9 left one repetition in reserve and RPE 10 left none; the scale worked on all three lifts in powerlifters.**

The scale pairs effort with repetitions in reserve (RIR): RPE 10 is 0 RIR and RPE 9 is 1 RIR. In 29 lifters, experienced squatters rated a 1RM higher than novices, and bar speed fell as RPE rose. In 15 powerlifters, RPE at 1RM was 9.6 to 9.7 on all three lifts, and RPE tracked percent of 1RM closely (r = 0.88 to 0.91).

- Rate each top set right after it ends, before looking at the bar speed or the numbers.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049), [Helms 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001517)

### Loading by RPE or bar speed works about as well as percentages

**Trials and a meta-analysis found no clear strength difference between autoregulated loading and fixed-percentage loading.**

A meta-analysis found no significant 1RM difference between autoregulated and standard percentage loading in resistance-trained people (mean difference 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46). In an 8-week trial of 21 trained men, RPE-based and percent-based loading both raised squat and bench press 1RM, and the gap between them was not significant. Both are valid ways to set load.

- Use RPE when daily readiness swings; use percentages when you want a fixed plan to compare weeks.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Hickmott 2022](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-021-00404-9), [Helms 2018](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00247), [Larsen 2021b](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.10663)

### Velocity loss limits did not change strength gains in a large review

**Ending a set when bar speed has dropped by a set percentage is a valid way to cap fatigue; the threshold changed strength little.**

A meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found the velocity loss chosen within sets did not change strength gains, while higher velocity loss went with more muscle growth. A second meta-analysis found thresholds of 25% or less gave slightly more 1RM strength (2.32 kg, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.31). Bar speed at 1RM differs by lift (0.23, 0.10 and 0.14 m/s for squat, bench and deadlift in 15 powerlifters), so each lift needs its own profile.

- Record bar speed on your own lifts for several weeks before using a velocity cut-off.

RPE and velocity · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Jukic 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01754-4), [Hickmott 2022](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-021-00404-9), [Helms 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001517)

### Strength does not need sets taken to failure

**Stopping sets short of failure gave similar strength gains to failure training, so heavy work can end with repetitions in reserve.**

A meta-analysis of 8 studies found non-failure training gave a 0.6 to 1.3% larger strength increase than failure training, a gap the authors judged unlikely to be meaningful. A later meta-regression found a negligible link between reps in reserve and strength gain, although muscle growth did show a negative slope with reps in reserve, meaning more growth nearer failure.

- Stop heavy sets with 1-3 repetitions in reserve; a missed rep costs recovery and, on the platform, a lift.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Davies 2016](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0451-3), [Robinson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02069-2)

### More weekly sets build more strength, with sharply diminishing returns

**Strength rises with weekly sets and with training frequency, but the gains flatten faster than muscle growth does.**

A meta-regression of 67 studies (2,058 participants) found strength gains rose with weekly set volume and with frequency, with diminishing returns that were more pronounced for strength than for muscle size. An earlier meta-analysis found high weekly sets beat low weekly sets (effect size 0.18), and a frequency meta-analysis found no significant effect once volume was equated.

- Add sets only when progress stalls, and add them to the lift that is lagging.

Frequency and volume · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Pelland 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w), [Ralston 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0762-7), [Ralston 2018](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-018-0149-9)

### A small dose of heavy work can still raise a powerlifter's 1RM

**About 3 to 6 heavy working sets per lift each week was enough to expect strength gains in powerlifters over 6 to 12 weeks.**

A multi-part study (interviews, surveys and two interventions with 25 intermediate to advanced powerlifters) proposed a minimum effective dose: about 3 to 6 working sets of 1 to 5 repetitions per lift each week, spread over 1 to 3 sessions, at loads above 80% of 1RM and RPE 7.5 to 9.5, for 6 to 12 weeks. It describes a floor for busy periods, not an ideal.

- Use this dose in busy or injured weeks, not as a long-term plan.

Frequency and volume · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655)

### Training days per week usually rise with level

**Beginners do well on 2 to 3 sessions a week; advanced lifters often spread the lifts across 4 to 6.**

For beginners there is trial evidence: a meta-analysis of 140 strength studies found untrained people gained most when each muscle group was trained 3 days a week, and trained people at 2. Past that it is coaching convention. Intermediates commonly train 3 to 4 days, with each lift twice a week. In a survey of 117 Norwegian powerlifters that included world, European and national champions, the most common answer (58.1%) was 5 to 6 sessions a week, with the most common load at 71-80% of 1RM.

- Add a session only when recovery between sessions is good and the lifts are improving.

Frequency and volume · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Shaw 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003584), [Rhea 2003](https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000053727.63505.d4)

### Planned variation beats a fixed routine for 1RM strength

**Periodised programs raised 1RM more than non-periodised ones, including when total volume was matched.**

A meta-analysis of 18 studies (81 effects) found periodised training gave larger 1RM gains than non-periodised training (effect size 0.43). A later meta-analysis of 35 volume-equated studies agreed for strength (effect size 0.31) but found no difference for muscle size. These trials were short, so the long-term picture in elite lifters is less clear.

- Change volume and intensity on a plan, not at random.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Well supported · Sources: [Williams 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0734-y), [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)

### Linear, block and undulating plans differ little in trials

**No clear winner between linear and undulating models; too few trials exist to compare block models.**

Linear plans raise load week by week, block plans stack phases (volume, then intensity, then peaking), and daily undulating plans vary reps and load between sessions. A meta-analysis of 17 studies (510 participants) found no difference between linear and undulating for strength. A later one found a small edge for undulating in trained people (effect size 0.61, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.22) and could not compare other models.

- Pick the model you will follow for a full cycle and judge it on your own logbook.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Harries 2015](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000000712), [Moesgaard 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01636-1)

### Lifters taper for 5 to 10 days by cutting volume and keeping heavy singles

**Surveys report a short step taper: volume down about 40-50%, intensity kept high, last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out.**

These are self-reports, not trials proving a taper works. In 364 North American raw powerlifters, a step taper over 7 to 10 days with 41-50% less volume was typical, with full rest about 2.8 days before the meet. A small trial of 19 athletes found 3 or 5 days of full rest kept lower-body strength; upper-body strength held at 3 days but not 5. A review found limited evidence that a short, heavy, low-volume session in the 48 hours before competition can help performance.

- Cut volume sharply but keep the competition lifts and a few heavy singles.
- Rest fully for the last 2 to 3 days before the meet.

Periodisation and peaking · Advanced · Thin evidence · Sources: [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177), [Winwood 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-026-02500-w), [Travis 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004183), [Harrison 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01136-3)

### Most strength athletes deload for about a week every 5 to 6 weeks

**Deloading is common but little tested: athletes cut sets and load, keep frequency and exercises, and add reps in reserve.**

An expert Delphi (34 coaches began, 21 finished the third round) defined a deload as a period of reduced training stress to mitigate fatigue and promote recovery. A survey of 246 strength and physique athletes found all deloaded, typically for 6.4 days every 5.6 weeks, keeping frequency and exercises. No trial has yet shown the best length or timing.

- Plan a lighter week roughly every 5 to 6 weeks, and move it earlier when joints ache and performance stalls.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Bell 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0), [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y)

### Low-bar squats lean forward and load the hips; high-bar squats stay upright

**Bar position changes the squat: low-bar uses more hip and back, high-bar more knee and quadriceps.**

A review of back squat biomechanics found high-bar squats showed more knee bend, less hip bend, a more upright torso and greater depth. Low-bar squats showed more hip bend and forward lean, with more erector spinae, adductor and gluteal activity. A systematic review of classic powerlifting research suggested low-bar squats generally let lifters move more weight.

- Try each position for several weeks and keep the one you can repeat at competition depth.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Glassbrook 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000002007), [Ferland 2019](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003099)

### Build the bench from the setup: tight back, planted feet, paused bar

**A stable arch and tight upper back shorten the bar path and make the pause on the chest repeatable.**

This is coaching convention. Keep head, shoulders and buttocks on the bench and feet flat on the floor. Pull the shoulder blades together and down, grip with the thumbs around the bar, and lower under control to the lower chest. Pause until the press command, then press back over the shoulders. Wider grips shorten the range, but federations cap grip width, so check the rulebook.

- Pause every training rep until the bar is still, and sometimes hold longer: the referee decides when to call 'Press'.

Technique and leverages · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [IPF 2026a](https://www.powerlifting.sport/rules/codes/info/technical-rules)

### Sumo and conventional deadlifts load the joints differently

**Sumo uses a wide stance and a more upright trunk; conventional moves the bar farther and does more mechanical work.**

In a video analysis of 12 sumo and 12 conventional lifters at a national championship, sumo lifters used a wider stance (70 cm against 32 cm; about 28 against 13 in), turned the feet out more and kept a more upright trunk. Bar distance, mechanical work and predicted energy cost were about 25 to 40% greater for conventional. The study did not test which style lifts more.

- Test both styles for a few weeks and keep the one that moves more weight with a steady back.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Escamilla 2000](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-200007000-00013)

### Limb and torso lengths change which set-up suits you

**Proportions shift the best stance, depth and grip, so copy principles from top lifters and not their exact positions.**

This is coaching convention, not a tested rule. Long thighs relative to the torso are thought to tip the squat forward and favour a wider stance. The one direct test, in 11 men squatting to parallel, found that ankle mobility went with trunk angle and segment-length ratios did not. Long arms shorten the pull in the deadlift and lengthen the bench press path; short arms do the reverse. Use these as starting guesses and let filmed sets and bar speed decide.

- Film from the side and compare two set-ups on the same weight before changing for good.
- If your squat folds forward, check ankle mobility before blaming your proportions.

Technique and leverages · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Fuglsang 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000001872)

### Choose accessories for the point where the lift slows or fails

**Find where the bar slows, then train the muscles and positions that fail there with 1 to 3 exercises.**

A review describes the sticking point as the position in the range where difficulty rises disproportionately, and says working out its cause helps choose training. Powerlifters in a minimum-dose study typically used 1 to 3 accessory exercises per lift at RPE 7 to 9 and about 6 to 10 repetitions.

- Film a slow or missed rep, locate the sticking point, then pick exercises that train that range.

Accessories and bands · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Kompf 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-016-0615-9), [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655)

### Bands and chains help trained lifters when loads are 80% of 1RM or more

**In a meta-analysis, variable resistance beat constant resistance for trained lifters at 80% of 1RM and above.**

A meta-analysis of 14 studies found variable-resistance training (bands or chains) beat constant resistance for maximum strength (effect size 0.80). In trained people the benefit appeared at 80% of 1RM or more (0.76) and not below (0.00). In surveys, 39% of 28 elite British lifters used bands and 57% chains, and 76.9% of 117 Norwegian lifters used variable resistance.

- Add bands or chains to heavy work once the base technique is stable.

Accessories and bands · Advanced · Some support · Sources: [Lin 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19148559), [Swinton 2009](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e31819424bd), [Shaw 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003584)

### Pick the class you can hold in training; move up when cutting costs lifts

**A lifter whose normal weight sits at a class limit can compete there with little cutting; large cuts are a reason to move up.**

This is coaching convention. Consider moving up when making weight takes more than a modest, gradual diet, when training quality drops in the weeks before weigh-in, or when you are growing into the next class anyway. An ACSM consensus statement on weight-category sports advises classifying athletes by preseason body composition and shortening the gap between weigh-in and competition.

- Weigh yourself in the morning for several weeks and compare the trend with the class limit.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Burke 2021](https://doi.org/10.1249/JSR.0000000000000831)

### Rapid weight cuts are common in powerlifting, and fluid loss costs strength

**Many lifters cut weight, mostly by fluid methods; fluid loss lowers strength and can harm health.**

Among 64 lifters at the 2018 IPF classic worlds, 83% cut weight (average 2.9% of body mass) and most reported negative effects on mood. In a survey of 321 lifters, 85.8% used rapid weight loss, and doctors and dietitians were rarely an influence. A meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts found hypohydration cut muscle strength by 5.5% on average. Extreme cuts can harm health; involve a sports dietitian or a doctor.

- Do not use fluid restriction, sauna or laxatives to make weight.
- Ask a sports dietitian or doctor before any planned weight loss.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199), [Nolan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000003488), [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0)

### Short sleep lowers performance, with evening sessions hit harder

**A meta-analysis found sleep loss cut exercise performance by about 7.6% on average.**

Across 69 publications, sleep loss (6 hours or less in 24) lowered performance by a mean of 7.56% (95% CI -11.9 to -3.13), including strength tasks. Tests done in the morning were largely unaffected; those done in the evening were consistently worse. A systematic review of 17 studies found several nights of restricted sleep could cut force in compound lifts.

- Protect sleep in the week before a meet and keep a normal bedtime.

Recovery and injuries · Beginner · Well supported · Sources: [Craven 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y), [Knowles 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012)

### Injury rates look low, but most lifters report pain in the back, shoulder or hip

**Counted as time lost, injuries are infrequent; counted as pain that affects training, most lifters have one.**

A systematic review of 9 studies found 1.0 to 4.4 injuries per 1,000 training hours in powerlifting, with the spine, shoulder and knee most affected. A survey of 104 Swedish subelite lifters counted pain or impaired function and found 70% currently injured and 87% injured in the past year, mostly lumbopelvic, shoulder and hip; only 16% of those currently injured stopped training completely.

- See a physio or doctor for pain that lasts more than a week, and adjust loads while it settles.

Recovery and injuries · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Aasa 2017](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096037), [Strömbäck 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967118771016)

## Common mistakes

### Testing a true max every few weeks

**Frequent max attempts add fatigue and risk without adding much information.**

This is coaching convention. A true max is the heaviest single you can complete with legal technique. It is a hard, slow-to-recover effort, and a bad day gives a misleading number. Work from a training max set from recent RPE 8 to 9 sets, and keep true maxes for meets or planned tests every few months.

- Test at a meet or a planned test day, not on impulse.

Percentages and zones · Intermediate · Coaching practice

### Running percentages off an old or lucky max

**A percentage is only as good as the max behind it, so reset the number when strength changes.**

This is coaching convention. If the max is months old, the percentages are too light or too heavy, and a lucky one-off single makes the plan too hard to finish. Reps at a given percentage also vary between lifters, so use RPE alongside the plan and rebase when weights feel clearly off.

- Rebase percentages after every cycle using your best recent set, not one lucky rep.

Percentages and zones · Beginner · Coaching practice

### Treating RPE as exact when most lifters misjudge reps in reserve

**People tend to underpredict reps left in the tank, so RPE is a rough guide that improves with practice.**

A meta-analysis of 12 studies (414 participants) found people underpredicted repetitions to failure by 0.95 reps on average, with wide variation. Accuracy improved when the prediction was made nearer failure, with heavier loads and in later sets. A set called RPE 8 may have been closer to RPE 9.

- Calibrate by comparing your RPE with bar speed or filmed sets over several weeks.

RPE and velocity · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Halperin 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01559-x)

### Cutting weight with fluid restriction in the last days

**Fluid restriction is a common but risky way to make weight, and it lowers strength and endurance.**

In the 2018 IPF classic worlds survey, fluid restriction after fluid loading was among the most common methods, used by about a third of lifters, alongside fasting and laxatives. A meta-analysis found hypohydration lowered muscle strength by 5.5% and muscle endurance by 8.3%. Where weigh-in is within about two hours of lifting, there is little time to recover.

- Stay near your class limit with normal eating, and see a sports dietitian before any cut.

Weight class and cutting · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0), [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199)

### Changing technique, equipment or exercises in the final weeks

**Late novelty brings soreness and risk with no time to adapt; keep the final weeks specific and familiar.**

This is coaching convention, and tapering interviews match it. Ten Croatian champions reported taper training that was highly specific, with assistance exercises removed and the same equipment as in competition. New Zealand elite lifters said poor tapers happened when they took a week or more off.

- Wear competition gear in the last heavy sessions and drop new exercises.

Periodisation and peaking · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [Grgic 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001699), [Pritchard 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001292)

## Key numbers

| Number | What it is | Support | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~5 reps (most lifts) | Repetitions possible at 90% of 1RM: Typical maximum reps at 90% 1RM across exercises; the bench press averaged about 4. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024a](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| ~14 reps (bench press) | Repetitions possible at 70% of 1RM on the bench: Typical maximum reps for the bench press at 70% 1RM; about 9 at 80% and about 4 at 90%. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024a](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| 2.5 reps (SD) | Spread in reps between lifters at 80% of 1RM: The between-lifter standard deviation at 80% 1RM is 2.51 reps, so the same percentage gives different rep counts. | Well supported | [Nuzzo 2024a](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7) |
| 40-50 % less volume | Volume cut during a taper: Surveyed North American powerlifters cut volume by 41-50%; a review of self-reported tapers gave about 40-45%. | Thin evidence | [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177), [Winwood 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-026-02500-w) |
| 7-10 days before the meet | Last heavy squat and deadlift before a meet: Most surveyed North American raw lifters did their final heavy squat and deadlift 7 to 10 days out; bench came later. | Thin evidence | [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177) |
| 3-6 sets per lift per week | Weekly working sets for a minimum effective dose: A floor proposed for powerlifters: 3 to 6 sets of 1 to 5 reps per lift, at loads above 80% 1RM, for 6 to 12 weeks. | Thin evidence | [Androulakis-Korakakis 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.713655) |
| 6.4 days (every 5.6 weeks) | Typical deload length: Average deload length reported by 246 competitive strength and physique athletes, taken about every 5.6 weeks. | Thin evidence | [Rogerson 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00691-y) |
| 83 % of 64 lifters | Lifters who cut weight at the 2018 IPF classic worlds: Cutters lost an average of 2.9% of body mass; most reported negative mood effects. | Some support | [Kwan 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004199) |
| 5.5 % lower muscle strength | Strength lost with hypohydration: Average fall in muscle strength with hypohydration in a meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts; endurance fell 8.3%. | Some support | [Savoie 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0349-0) |
| 35 years (SD 7) | Mean age of peak performance in world-class powerlifters: From world championship results 2003-2017; powerlifters peaked about 9 years later than weightlifters. | Some support | [Solberg 2019](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2019-0093) |

## Intensity zones as a percent of 1RM

Common coaching zones with typical reps per set and their purpose; reps at a given percentage vary by lifter.

| Zone | % of 1RM | Typical reps per set | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light | 50-65% | 8-12 or more | Warm-ups, skill work, easy days |
| Moderate | 65-75% | 5-8 | Volume work and technique practice |
| Working | 75-85% | 3-6 | Main strength work |
| Heavy | 85-92% | 1-3 | Heavy strength work, peaking blocks, openers |
| Near-max | 92-100% | 1 | Singles, tests, second and third attempts |

Coaching practice · Sources: [Nuzzo 2024a](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-023-01937-7), [Travis 2021b](https://doi.org/10.1177/0031512520967608), [Howells 2022](https://doi.org/10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12140-1)

## RPE to reps in reserve chart

RPE 5 to 10 matched to repetitions in reserve (RIR); 9.5 is a half step many lifters add.

| RPE | Reps in reserve | What it feels like | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0 | No repetition left; a true limit | Max attempts, 1RM tests |
| 9.5 | 0-1 | No rep left, but you could add a little load | Heavy top singles |
| 9 | 1 | One more repetition was possible | Heavy top sets |
| 8 | 2 | Two more possible; bar speed still decent | Main working sets |
| 7 | 3 | Three more possible; fast and controlled | Volume work, easier days |
| 5-6 | 4-6 | Light; plenty left | Warm-ups, technique work |

Some support · Sources: [Zourdos 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001049), [Helms 2016](https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000218)

## A 12-week cycle outline

A common layout from base volume to meet week; adjust loads by RPE and your own recovery.

| Weeks | Phase | Main work | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-4 | Accumulation | More sets and reps at 65-80% of 1RM | RPE 6-8 |
| 5-8 | Intensification | Fewer reps at 75-90%; competition-style lifts | RPE 7-9 |
| 9-10 | Peaking | Heavy doubles and singles at 85-95%; practise commands | RPE 8-9 |
| 11 | Taper | Volume down 40-50%; last heavy squat and deadlift | RPE 7-8 |
| 12 | Meet week | Short, light sessions early; rest the last 2-3 days | RPE 5-7 |

Coaching practice

## Terms

- **Accessory exercise**: An exercise outside the three competition lifts, chosen to build a muscle or fix a weak point.
- **Daily undulating periodisation (DUP)**: A plan that varies rep ranges and loads between sessions within the week, such as heavy, medium and light days.
- **Deload**: A planned lighter week or block, with less volume or load, to clear fatigue between harder blocks.
- **One-repetition maximum (1RM)**: The heaviest weight you can lift once with legal technique; the base for percentage programming.
- **Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)**: A 1 to 10 rating of how hard a set was; in strength training it is tied to how many repetitions were left.
- **Repetitions in reserve (RIR)**: How many more clean repetitions you could have done when the set ended; 2 RIR means two more were possible.
- **Sticking point**: The position in a lift where the bar slows most or where failures happen.
- **Taper (peaking)**: A planned drop in training stress, mostly volume, in the last days or weeks before a meet so fatigue clears and strength shows.
- **Velocity-based training (VBT)**: Setting load or stopping sets from measured bar speed, using a device that reports mean concentric velocity in metres per second.
- **Working max (training max)**: A weight you can repeat on a normal day, often set below a true max, and used as the base for training percentages.

# Meet day: KiteSink fitness field guide

Your first competition, in order. Each entry gives the point, the reasoning, what to do, how well supported it is, and its sources.

## Guidance

### Classes, gear lists and drug testing differ between federations

**IPF has 8 classes per sex; USA Powerlifting and the USPA list 12 each; check the one you will enter.**

IPF men's classes run from 59 kg to 120+ kg and women's from 47 kg to 84+ kg, plus a lowest sub-junior and junior class of 53 kg (men) or 43 kg (women). USA Powerlifting has 12 classes per sex (men 52 to 140+ kg, women 44 to 100+ kg). The USPA lists 12 (men 52 to 140.1+ kg, women 44 to 110+ kg). Gear must meet the federation's lists, and testing rules differ.

- Check the class table, then the rulebook, of the federation that runs your meet.

Federation and entry · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Three referees show white or red lights, then cards give the reason

**White means good lift and red means no lift; after the lights come up, cards show why a lift was turned down.**

In IPF rules each referee controls a white and a red light, and the lights come on together. A red, blue or yellow card (1, 2, 3) shows the reason for a failure. Common reasons: squat depth, double bounce or not standing erect, stepping and missed commands. Bench: bar not reaching the chest or elbows not low enough, downward movement or no lockout, heaving and missed commands. Deadlift: knees or shoulders not locked, supporting the bar on the thighs, lowering early or losing control.

- Ask your coach to note the card colours so you can fix the cause.

Platform and lights · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/)

### You can change an opener once; second attempts and bench or squat thirds are locked

**You submit each next weight within one minute of the lights; after that, changes are tightly limited.**

IPF: one change on the first attempt of each lift, higher or lower, up to three minutes before the first round starts for the first group. Second attempts and third attempts in squat and bench cannot be changed. In the third deadlift round you may change twice unless the bar has been called loaded. Weights are multiples of 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) and rise by at least 2.5 kg. If you miss, you may take that weight again, but only in the next round. USA Powerlifting uses the same structure.

- Give your coach the written plan, the minimum increment, and who submits the card.

Attempts and warm-up · Intermediate · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/)

### Caffeine gave a small strength gain in upper-body lifts

**A meta-analysis of 10 strength studies found a small gain overall, clearer for upper-body strength.**

Caffeine improved strength (standardised mean difference 0.20, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.36) and power. For upper-body strength the effect was 0.21 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.39); for lower-body strength it was 0.15 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.34), not clearly different from zero. Effects differ between people and the evidence in women is thin. Caffeine lasted longer in women on low-dose oral contraceptives, with a half-life of about 7.9 hours against 5.4 in non-users. Avoid trying it for the first time at a meet.

- Try your planned dose in training before the meet.

Attempts and warm-up · Intermediate · Some support · Sources: [Grgic 2018](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-018-0216-0), [Abernethy 1985](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00544361)

### Aim for nine good lifts and a smooth day, not a personal record

**A first meet is practice for the whole day: weigh-in, warm-ups, commands and timing.**

Choose an opener that you could lift easily, take a realistic second and add a third only if the second felt solid. Good first-meet goals are hitting all commands, making nine good lifts and learning the flow of a meet. Records and totals come later. Bring a coach or friend who can read the flight order and keep the attempt plan.

- Set two process goals, such as clean commands and on-time warm-ups.

Attempts and warm-up · Beginner · Coaching practice

### Tested meets use drug testing; untested meets may not

**A federation or meet name tells you which one it is; tested and untested results are kept separate.**

USA Powerlifting competes members who have not used performance-enhancing drugs for 36 months and can test members at any time. The USPA allows meet directors to run tested meets with approval, labels them 'Tested' and keeps results and records separate from untested meets. Which one you choose changes who you compete against and whether records count. This is not advice on medicines; ask a doctor if you take any prescription.

- Check whether a meet is tested before you register.

Federation and entry · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

## Common mistakes

### Opening with a weight that is nearly a max

**An opener that is hard to lift risks all three attempts and the total. At a first meet, open lighter, at about 85% of your best single or a little less.**

Elite classic lifters opened near 91% of their expected third attempt, and in 10,672 Australian raw entries squat openers averaged 92% of the best squat made that day. These data do not separate first meets. McDonald's rule for a first-timer is lighter: a weight you could squat for five clean reps on a bad day, about 80 to 85 percent, and lower still on the bench because of the pause and commands. A miss uses one of three tries, and a made opener means you cannot bomb out of that lift.

- At a first meet, open with a weight you could use as your last warm-up.
- With meet experience, choose an opener from your best recent single, then drop it a little if unsure.

Attempts and warm-up · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Travis 2021b](https://doi.org/10.1177/0031512520967608), [McDonald 2021a](https://bodyrecomposition.com/powerlifting/6-tips-first-powerlifting-meet), [Howells 2022](https://doi.org/10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12140-1)

### Arriving with gear you never checked against the rulebook

**Gear that is not on the list, is too long or too thick, or is torn gets rejected at the equipment check.**

IPF inspectors reject unclean or torn items and gear outside the stated limits, such as a belt over 10 cm (3.9 in) wide or sleeves over 7 mm thick. An item found illegal on the platform after inspection can lead to disqualification. USA Powerlifting requires an equipment check for every competitor. Hats are not allowed on the platform in IPF rules.

- Compare every item with the rulebook two weeks before the meet.

Classes and equipment · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/)

### Missing your call because the warm-up ran long

**You have one minute to start your attempt after the bar is called ready; a late start forfeits it.**

IPF: the lifter has one minute from the speaker's call to start the attempt, or the attempt is forfeited. Warm-ups that start too early leave you cold and bored; too late and you walk to the platform rushed. Count lifters ahead of you, use the board, and ask staff when unsure.

- Finish the last warm-up several lifters before your opener.
- Check rack height before you are called.

Attempts and warm-up · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)

### Trying new food or a big meal after weigh-in

**A large or unfamiliar meal after weigh-in can leave you full or ill when the first squat comes.**

Familiar food is the safe choice. A review of 49 carbohydrate studies found no clear acute strength gain from extra carbohydrate in most cases, so there is little reason to experiment on the day. Eat what has worked on a heavy training day, and keep portions moderate.

- Rehearse your meet-day meals on a heavy training day.

Weigh-in and food · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Henselmans 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu14040856)

## In order

### Choose a federation: tested or untested sets who you lift against

**Tested federations drug test lifters; untested ones do not. The federation also sets your rules, classes and gear list.**

USA Powerlifting limits competition to members who have not used performance-enhancing drugs for 36 months before the meet, and members can be tested at any time. The USPA offers tested meets only with national office approval, labels them 'Tested' and keeps their results separate from untested meets. IPF coaches in the warm-up and lifting area must acknowledge the IPF Anti-Doping Rules. Classes and gear lists differ, so read the rulebook of the federation you enter.

- Find the federation's meet calendar and read its current rulebook before you enter.

Months out · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Register, then pick a class you can reach by normal eating

**Join the federation, enter the meet by its deadline and choose a class near your normal weight.**

USA Powerlifting memberships run from January 1 to December 31. USPA membership covers 12 months from the date of issue. Meets set their own entry forms, fees and deadlines. USPA requires ID and your membership card at weigh-in, and IPF weigh-in requires ID or a passport. Class limits differ between federations (see the class table), so check the one used by your meet.

- Read the meet's entry form for deadlines, fees and the weigh-in schedule.
- Choose the class you can hold with normal eating, not a cut.

Months out · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf), [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)

### Buy legal gear early and train in it

**In IPF rules you need a singlet, a T-shirt under it, shoes and shin-length socks for the deadlift; belt, sleeves and wraps are optional.**

IPF limits: belt up to 10 cm (3.9 in) wide and 13 mm (0.5 in) thick; knee sleeves up to 7 mm thick and 30 cm (11.8 in) long; wrist wraps up to 1 m (39 in) long and 8 cm (3.1 in) wide; shoe soles up to 5 cm (2 in). Hats are not allowed. Belts, singlets and sleeves must come from makers on the IPF Approved List. USA Powerlifting uses the same sleeve and wrist wrap limits. Wear all of it in the last heavy sessions.

- Check each item against your federation's approved list before you buy it.
- Wear the full kit for your last heavy sessions.

Weeks out · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [Grgic 2017](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001699)

### Plan nine attempts with your coach or a trusted friend

**Plan an opener you could lift easily on any day, a realistic second, and a hard but makeable third.**

Elite classic lifters at IPF World Championships opened near 91% of their expected third attempt, then added about 5% for the second and about 3% for the third. Across 10,672 raw entries in Australian meets, squat openers averaged 92% of the lifter's best squat that day. Base your plan on your best recent single, not on a hope. Write all nine weights down with a lighter plan B for each lift, and round to 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) steps.

- Use the attempt table below, and your best recent single, to fill in all nine weights.

Weeks out · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Travis 2021b](https://doi.org/10.1177/0031512520967608), [Howells 2022](https://doi.org/10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12140-1)

### Taper over the last week or two: less volume, a few heavy singles

**Survey data show a step taper with 41-50% less volume, the last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out, and rest in the last days.**

In 364 North American raw powerlifters, a step taper over 7 to 10 days with 41-50% less volume was typical. The last heavy squat and deadlift came 7 to 10 days out, the last heavy bench under 7 days out, and full rest about 2.8 days before the meet. In a small trial of 19 athletes, 3 days off kept upper- and lower-body strength; 5 days off cost upper-body strength. A review found limited evidence that a short, heavy, low-volume session within 48 hours of competition can help.

- Keep the lifts, cut the sets, and stop hard training about 3 days out.

The week before · Intermediate · Thin evidence · Sources: [Travis 2021a](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004177), [Travis 2022](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004183), [Harrison 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01136-3)

### Confirm the schedule, travel and food for the meet

**Know your session, weigh-in time and flight, and have travel and meals sorted before the last days.**

Find your session and flight on the meet schedule and confirm with the meet director. Book a bed close to the venue if the drive is long. Plan your food for the day before and the day of the meet, and pack the bag early. Squat and bench rack heights are written down at weigh-in, so measure yours in training.

- Pack the bag a few days early using the checklist below.
- Note your squat and bench rack heights and foot-block settings.

The week before · Beginner · Coaching practice

### Lay out gear, eat familiar food and sleep as normally as you can

**Eat meals that you know sit well, drink fluids steadily and avoid new foods or heavy training.**

Lay out singlet, T-shirt, socks, belt, shoes and ID. Skip new foods and alcohol. A poor night before a meet is common and a single night with little sleep had little effect on muscle strength in a systematic review of 17 studies, while several nights of restricted sleep could reduce force in compound lifts. Go to bed at your usual time and do not worry about one bad night.

- Keep the day light: a short walk and easy mobility at most.
- Go to bed at your normal time.

The day before · Beginner · Coaching practice · Sources: [Knowles 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012)

### Weigh in about two hours before lifting, with ID and your opening attempts

**IPF and USA Powerlifting weigh-ins run for 90 minutes and start two hours before lifting; the USPA can offer one up to 24 hours before.**

IPF: weigh-in no earlier than two hours before the start for a category and lasts one and a half hours; bring ID or a passport; opening attempts are declared at weigh-in. USA Powerlifting: weigh-in starts two hours before lifting, lasts 90 minutes and ends 30 minutes before lifting. USPA: weigh-in lasts at least 90 minutes, with an optional early weigh-in up to 24 hours before lifting. If you miss class weight, you may return to the scale within the window.

- Arrive early, bring ID and your written openers, and keep your gear bag with you.

Weigh-in · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Pass the equipment check and sign the rack height sheet

**Referees inspect and approve each item you plan to wear; an illegal item found later can disqualify you.**

IPF: at least two referees inspect gear any time up to 30 minutes before your category starts; unclean or torn items are rejected, and over-length wraps can be cut and resubmitted. If you appear on the platform with an illegal item, you are disqualified. USA Powerlifting: every competitor has an equipment check, normally during the weigh-in period, with a 30-minute deadline before the session. Check squat and bench rack heights and sign the sheet.

- Bring every item you plan to wear, including your belt and sleeves.
- Sign the rack height sheet after checking each height.

Weigh-in · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/)

### Eat and drink steadily after weigh-in, using food you know

**After weigh-in, eat a familiar meal and sip fluids, then keep snacks nearby for the rest of the day.**

Eat normal, familiar foods and avoid very large or high-fibre meals just before the first squat. A systematic review of 49 carbohydrate studies found extra carbohydrate did not improve acute performance in 13 studies, and helped in six, mainly in fasted lifters or workouts of more than 10 sets per muscle group. A meet day is long, so steady eating and drinking matters more than any single food.

- Eat a normal meal within an hour of weigh-in.
- Sip fluids across the morning instead of drinking a large amount at once.

Weigh-in · Beginner · Thin evidence · Sources: [Henselmans 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu14040856)

### Time your warm-up from the flight order, not the clock

**Work backwards from your opener: count the lifters ahead of you and finish your last warm-up a few lifters before your call.**

Check the board for the flight order and watch how fast the platform moves. A common plan is a general warm-up, then 4 to 6 ramping sets on the bar, with the last warm-up about three to four lifters before your opener. Under IPF rules a single group gets 20 minutes between lifts, and each lifter has one minute to start after being called. Ask a coach or loader if you are unsure how many lifters are left.

- Ask the warm-up room staff how many lifters are ahead of you every few minutes.
- Be ready at the platform area when the lifter before you takes the bar.

The warm-up room · Intermediate · Coaching practice · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)

### Squat: wait for the command, reach depth, wait for 'rack'

**After unracking, stand still with knees locked and wait for 'Squat'; squat below parallel, stand up, then wait for 'Rack'.**

IPF: step back, stand motionless with knees locked, and wait for the downward arm movement and 'Squat'. The top of the legs at the hip joint must go lower than the top of the knees, in one descent, then you rise with knees locked and wait for 'Rack'. If you are not in position after five seconds you hear 'Replace'. USA Powerlifting and the USPA use the same words. Foot movement, double bounces and missing a command can turn the lift down.

- Settle, take a breath and wait for the full command before you move.

On the platform · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Bench: wait for 'start', pause on the chest, wait for 'press'

**Lock the elbows and wait for 'Start'; lower the bar to your chest, hold still, wait for 'Press', then press and wait for 'Rack'.**

IPF: head, shoulders and buttocks stay on the bench and feet stay flat on the floor. Grip with thumbs around the bar and hands no wider than 81 cm (32 in) between the forefingers. After 'Start', the bar goes to the chest or abdominal area and the underside of the elbows reaches level with or below the shoulders. Hold motionless until 'Press', then lock the arms and wait for 'Rack'. USA Powerlifting and the USPA use the same words.

- Practise the pause on every training rep, with a count you can repeat.

On the platform · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Deadlift: pull to a full lockout and wait for 'down'

**Stand erect with knees locked and shoulders back and wait for 'Down'; then lower the bar with control.**

IPF, USA Powerlifting and USPA use one command, 'Down', given once the bar is held motionless at a full lockout. Reasons for a turn-down include downward movement of the bar before lockout, supporting the bar on the thighs, lowering it before the command, losing control with both hands, and stepping. Foot movement after the command is not a fault. In IPF and USA Powerlifting meets you may change a third-attempt deadlift twice, unless you were already called to a bar loaded to your submitted weight.

- Stand tall, hold the lockout for a beat, and wait for the command.

On the platform · Beginner · Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf), [USA Powerlifting 2026](https://www.usapowerlifting.com/technical/), [USPA 2025](https://uspa.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/USPA-Rulebook-March-24th-2025.pdf)

### Between flights: small snacks, fluids, and caffeine only if tried

**Eat and drink in small amounts between lifts and try any caffeine in training first.**

A meta-analysis of 10 strength studies found caffeine gave a small strength gain overall (standardised mean difference 0.20, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.36), clearer for the upper body than the lower body. Keep snacks small and familiar, and keep fluid steady. Caffeine affects people differently, so use only what you have used in training and stop if it causes jitters or an upset stomach.

- Eat a small familiar snack and sip fluid after each discipline.
- Use caffeine only in amounts you have tried in training.

Between lifts · Beginner · Some support · Sources: [Grgic 2018](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-018-0216-0)

### After the meet: results, food, rest and a review

**Collect your results, eat and rest, and review what the attempts taught you before you plan the next cycle.**

Ask for the score sheet and any video, and note which attempts were turned down and the reason shown on the cards. Eat and drink normally and take a few easy days before hard training starts. In tested federations you can be asked for a sample after lifting; follow the doping control officer's instructions. Write down what you would change about openers, warm-ups and food for the next meet.

- Write a short review the next day, while details are fresh.

Afterwards · Beginner · Coaching practice

| 59.0 kg: up to 59.0 kg | up to 130.1 lb | 47.0 kg: up to 47.0 kg | up to 103.6 lb |
| 66.0 kg: 59.01 to 66.0 kg | up to 145.5 lb | 52.0 kg: 47.01 to 52.0 kg | up to 114.6 lb |
| 74.0 kg: 66.01 to 74.0 kg | up to 163.1 lb | 57.0 kg: 52.01 to 57.0 kg | up to 125.7 lb |
| 83.0 kg: 74.01 to 83.0 kg | up to 183.0 lb | 63.0 kg: 57.01 to 63.0 kg | up to 138.9 lb |
| 93.0 kg: 83.01 to 93.0 kg | up to 205.0 lb | 69.0 kg: 63.01 to 69.0 kg | up to 152.1 lb |
| 105.0 kg: 93.01 to 105.0 kg | up to 231.5 lb | 76.0 kg: 69.01 to 76.0 kg | up to 167.6 lb |
| 120.0 kg: 105.01 to 120.0 kg | up to 264.6 lb | 84.0 kg: 76.01 to 84.0 kg | up to 185.2 lb |
| 120.0+ kg: over 120.0 kg | over 264.6 lb | 84.0+ kg: over 84.0 kg | over 185.2 lb |

Rulebook · Sources: [IPF 2026b](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)

## Platform commands for each lift

Commands as given by the chief referee in IPF, USA Powerlifting and USPA rules; wait for each one.

| Lift | Commands in order | What you do first | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squat | 'Squat', then 'Rack' | Stand erect, knees locked, motionless | Depth: top of legs at the hip below the top of the knees |
| Bench press | 'Start', 'Press', 'Rack' | Arms locked and still for 'Start'; bar still on chest for 'Press' | Elbows level with or below the shoulders at the chest |
| Deadlift | 'Down' | Stand erect, knees locked, shoulders back | One command, given once the lockout is held |
| Squat or bench | 'Replace' | Fix the reason the referee gives you | IPF: if not in position after five seconds |

## Attempt selection ranges, first meet and experienced

Ranges as a share of a current best single, with a 200 kg (441 lb) example. Experienced rows follow meet data; first-meet rows follow McDonald, as no study covers first meets.

| Attempt | % of current best single | Example at 200 kg (441 lb) | Aim |
|---|---|---|---|
| First-meet opener | 80-85% | 160-170 kg (353-375 lb) | A weight that feels like a last warm-up |
| First-meet second | 85-92% | 170-184 kg (375-406 lb) | Close to a best triple |
| First-meet third | 92-95% | 184-190 kg (406-419 lb) | About a best double, not a max |
| Opener | 88-92% | 176-184 kg (388-406 lb) | A weight you could lift easily on any day |
| Second | 94-97.5% | 188-195 kg (414-430 lb) | A solid, realistic lift |
| Third | 98-102.5% | 196-205 kg (432-452 lb) | A hard but makeable attempt |

## Meet bag checklist

Pack in the days before the meet, and check the rules of your federation for each item.

**Required to lift**

- Singlet
- T-shirt to wear under the singlet
- Shin-length socks for the deadlift
- Lifting shoes or deadlift slippers
- Photo ID or passport
- Federation membership card

**Optional gear (if your federation allows)**

- Belt (IPF: up to 10 cm / 3.9 in wide, 13 mm thick)
- Knee sleeves (up to 7 mm thick, 30 cm / 11.8 in long)
- Wrist wraps (up to 1 m / 39 in long, 8 cm / 3.1 in wide)
- Chalk or baby powder, if the meet allows it
- Medical tape for thumbs (IPF: two layers at most)

**Paperwork and plan**

- Entry confirmation and the meet schedule
- Written plan for all nine attempts
- Squat and bench rack heights and foot-block settings
- Pen and notebook

**Food and drink**

- Familiar meal for after weigh-in
- Small snacks for between flights
- Water or a drink you have used in training
- Caffeine only if you have tried it in training

**Comfort and recovery**

- Spare T-shirt and socks
- Towel
- Warm layer for the warm-up room
- Phone charger
- A friend or coach to hand up attempt cards

Coaching practice

## Terms

- **Bomb out**: To miss all three attempts on a lift; in a full-power meet that usually means no total.
- **Chief referee**: The referee who gives the commands on the platform; two side referees also judge each lift.
- **Classic (raw)**: A division with a non-supportive singlet and no supportive suits, shirts or knee wraps; belt, knee sleeves and wrist wraps are allowed within limits.
- **Flight (group)**: A group of lifters who take their attempts together; larger sessions split into flights, with lower previous totals lifting first in IPF rules.
- **Lot number**: A number drawn at weigh-in; if two lifters choose the same weight, the lower lot number lifts first.
- **Opener (first attempt)**: The first of your three attempts on a lift; chosen to be easy enough that you lift it with room to spare.
- **Rack height sheet**: The form where you record squat and bench rack and foot-block settings at weigh-in, so loaders set them before your attempt.
- **Spotter/loaders**: Helpers who load the bar and spot squat and bench; two to five are on the platform at a time in IPF rules.
